works.abstract: Neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), a lethal outcome of androgen deprivation, arises through neuroendocrine transdifferentiation (NEtD) of prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), yet its initiating drivers and their temporal order remain only partially defined. Clinical single-cell studies primarily capture established PRAD or NEPC at single timepoints, so they cannot directly resolve transitional states or the order and direction of transdifferentiation. We generated longitudinal single-cell RNA sequencing of the LTL331 patient-derived xenograft across eight timepoints spanning pre-castration PRAD to relapsed NEPC (51,726 cells) with matched whole-exome sequencing, integrating inferred single-cell copy-number profiles, trajectory inference, regulon and transcription-factor-activity analysis, and chromatin-accessibility data from a clinical metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer atlas. Lineage states were tested for replication in two clinical single-cell cohorts by embedding-free, label-level comparison. NEtD proceeded by transcriptional reprogramming of a single clone, not clonal outgrowth: PRAD and NEPC shared copy-number architecture and a truncal TMPRSS2 :: ERG rearrangement, with the androgen receptor ( AR ) locus copy-number stable despite loss of AR transcription. Every PRAD-to-NEPC path funneled through one transient, obligate mesenchymal gateway (~0.25% of cells, peaking 12–16 weeks post-castration) that re-engaged the early neural-crest program in developmental order: the neural-plate-border regulator MSX1 peaked with the EMT-delamination program, and border specifier PAX7 persisted into the early neuroendocrine state. From this gateway the lineage bifurcated with strong bias toward a tuft-negative ASCL1− fate (≈0.94 versus ≈0.06; paired p = 4.8 × 10 −23 ; POU2F3 < 1%), diverging from the canonical ASCL1 / PHOX2B route and the ASCL1 -versus-tuft split of other NEPC models. MSX1 is a candidate priming regulator, supported by transcription-factor-activity analysis and AR−/NE+-specific footprints in patient NEPC chromatin. Adenocarcinoma and ASCL1 + neuroendocrine programs replicated in patient cohorts (AUROC 0.82–0.83), and neuroendocrine identity tracked the clinical neuroendocrine-differentiation (odds ratios 134.6 and 31.4). In the LTL331 patient-derived model, NEtD is a directional, stepwise transition rather than a stochastic loss of identity. To our knowledge, this study provides the first time-resolved evidence that prostate NEtD re-engages the early neural-crest program in developmental order before committing to a predominantly ASCL1− fate. The obligate gateway is a potential opportunity for intervention, and its regulators are candidate targets for intercepting NEtD. Not applicable.

works.title: WinPopLDdecay: a hardware-adaptive and reproducible reimplementation of PopLDdecay with a graphical interface
Thyra: bridging mass spectrometry imaging and SpatialData for unified multimodal analysis
Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain
Aptamer-mediated multivalent endogenous ADAR1 recruitment for highly efficient RNA editing
works.abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)—an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. By optimizing aptamers targeting the Zα domain of ADAR1 p150 and embedding them in a circular RNA scaffold, MARRS enables near-complete adenosine-to-inosine editing of RNA targets in cultured cells and mouse models, achieving efficiencies up to 100% in vitro and 84% in vivo. MARRS also exhibits remarkable versatility across a range of transcript targets while maintaining high specificity with minimal off-target effects. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform. The multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system (MARRS) is an RNA editing platform that efficiently recruits endogenous ADAR1 to achieve precise adenosine-to-inosine editing. MARRS enables up to 100% editing in vitro and 84% in vivo with high specificity across diverse RNA targets.

works.title: CopilotJ: a conversational multi-agent system for intelligent and efficient bioimage analysis
Author Correction: Prediction of protein subcellular localization in single cells
The Gujarat Tribal Genome Project (2kTGP)
Decoupling cis and trans transcriptional influences
A ubiquitin network safeguards cell identity by continuously degrading a stem cell-related translational machinery
works.abstract: midgut, we identified a posttranscriptional regulatory layer that supervises enterocyte (EC) identity and fails upon aging. Combining single-cell RNA-seq with lineage tracing in aging ECs and classical genetics, we found that aging ECs express genes that unlock the differentiated state. Upon aging, the protein Rogue (CG13928), a translational repressor, along with its partner, Orb2, orchestrates reactivation of a stem cell-related translational repression machinery involving P-body-associated RNA-binding proteins canceling the differentiated state. In young ECs, this machinery is continuously suppressed by the deubiquitinase nonstop (dUSP22) and the ubiquitin E2 dUbcH8/Kdo and E3 CTLH complex, mediating the degradation of the stem cell-related RNA binding proteins safeguarding EC identity. Upon aging, levels of dUSP22 decline and Rogue is ectopically expressed. RNA immunoprecipitation followed by nanopore-based direct RNA sequencing identified that Rogue binds to the RNA transcripts of dUbcH8/Kdo and eEF2, shortening their poly(A) tail and suppressing Kdo protein, resulting in accelerated proteasomal clearance of the CTLH complex. Subsequently, the stem cell-related P-bodies are reactivated, leading to decline in EC gene signatures and unlocking EC identity.

works.title: The glutamine-aspartate metabolic tradeoff between fast growth and metabolic flexibility
works.abstract: Abstract Background Cancer cells develop selective dependencies on nutrients, creating potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention. However, how metabolic rewiring enables cancer cells to sustain proliferation while adapting to nutrient limitation remains incompletely understood. Results We develop a systematic framework to investigate nutrient dependencies and apply it to extracellular glutamine dependence. By measuring metabolite exchange rates across 54 cancer cell lines with different degrees of glutamine dependence, together with metabolic profiling of human stem-cell differentiation, we identify tissue-associated differences in the use of glutamine and aspartate for glutamate biosynthesis. These differences are linked to a trade-off between rapid proliferation and metabolic flexibility. Time-resolved intracellular metabolomics following glutamine withdrawal reveal a common limitation in purine biosynthesis. However, this metabolic limitation alone is insufficient to explain glutamine dependency, suggesting that additional regulatory responses to glutamine deprivation contribute to growth arrest. Conclusions Our study provides a systematic framework for identifying metabolic features associated with nutrient dependence and shows how established functions of glutamine, aspartate and asparagine are coordinated across diverse cancer cell types. This approach may support the mechanistic characterization and pharmacological targeting of metabolic dependencies beyond glutamine addiction.

works.title: Mitigating bias in spatial transcriptomic pipelines via human feedback with CSDE
works.abstract: Abstract Biological discovery from large-scale assays requires extensive preprocessing, during which raw outputs (e.g., images, sequences) are processed into structured forms amenable to analysis. In spatial transcriptomics, differential expression analysis depends on cell segmentation, gene expression quantification, and cell-type annotation, all prone to systematic errors. We introduce corrected spatial differential expression (CSDE), building on prediction-powered inference to leverage a small set of expert-validated cells to correct for preprocessing bias. Across three case studies, CSDE yields more reliable differential expression estimates than the prevalent approach neglecting preprocessing.

works.title: ArthroVerse: mapping protein family diversity across arthropod-associated microbiomes
works.abstract: Metagenomic studies of arthropod-associated microbiomes have generated vast amounts of sequence data, yet the functional and structural organization of these proteins remains largely unexplored. Here, we present ArthroVerse, the first comprehensive database of protein families derived from arthropod-associated metagenomes. Non-redundant protein families were generated after rigorous filtering, deduplication, and clustering. The protein families were further annotated with microbial taxonomy, host associations, protein structural information, and carbohydrate-active enzymes predictions. The resulting dataset integrates both metagenomic and reference genome-derived proteins, enabling systematic exploration of functional diversity, evolutionary relationships, and host-microbe interactions in insect microbiomes. ArthroVerse provides a valuable resource for the study of microbial ecology and arthropod physiology, offering unprecedented insight into the protein landscape of insect-associated microbial communities. ArthroVerse is publicly accessible at https://envofams.org/arthroverse/.

works.title: SynBioFooDB: a comprehensive resource for synthetic biology-driven food biomanufacturing
works.abstract: Enabled by synthetic biology and metabolic engineering, microbial biomanufacturing is reshaping the production of food-related compounds by offering sustainable alternatives to resource-intensive extraction and conventional chemical synthesis. However, information linking food-related compounds to biosynthetic pathways and microbial biomanufacturing evidence remains fragmented across the literature and poorly represented in existing food-oriented resources, hindering cross-study comparison, evidence synthesis, and rational design of microbial production systems. Here, we present SynBioFooDB (https://synbiofoodb.biodesign.ac.cn/), a knowledgebase dedicated to synthetic biology-driven food biomanufacturing. SynBioFooDB integrates 74 237 food-related compounds with standardized chemical identities and annotations covering food occurrence, bioactivity, toxicity, and regulatory information. It further provides expert-curated biomanufacturing evidence for 1054 compounds from 5592 publications, linking microbial hosts, substrates, genetic modifications, and quantitative production metrics through structured and traceable records. The database also contains 2002 literature-reported biosynthetic pathways for 971 compounds, enabling comparison of alternative precursors, enzyme combinations, and pathway architectures. For compounds without literature-reported pathways, SynBioFooDB provides computationally predicted candidate pathways to facilitate pathway prioritization and experimental evaluation. By integrating compound-level context, biomanufacturing evidence, and biosynthetic pathway information, SynBioFooDB supports systematic exploration, comparison, and rational design of microbial production strategies for food-related compounds.

works.title: KEGG for characterizing genomes and pathways in the biosphere
works.abstract: The KEGG database (https://www.kegg.jp) has been developed as a model of the biological systems. By organizing knowledge of cellular and organism-level functions in the form of molecular wiring diagrams, the model enables generating new knowledge and finding practical applications. The KO (KEGG Orthology) dataset plays the basic role of organizing knowledge. KO is an ortholog with functional relevance, generalizing experimental evidence in specific organisms to other organisms. KEGG molecular networks, including pathway maps and modules, are generic networks with KOs as network nodes, and thus KEGG mapping from genomes to pathways can be applied to any organism. As the number of KOs increases and the KO annotation rate improves, KEGG mapping is further expanded. A set of KOs in the genome and a set of modules in the metabolic pathways are now used to characterize various data objects in the biosphere, including organisms, organism groups, microbiomes, viruses, and their combinations, such as endosymbiont-host, microbiome-host, and virus-host relationships. Furthermore, a simple measure of similarity either by KO compositions or module compositions is introduced to compare organism groups. The resulting similarity dendrograms possibly reflect similarity of cellular functions or, more specifically, metabolic functions, which can be compared with phylogenetic trees.

works.title: SureChEMBL in 2026: an open database of chemical and biomedical annotations from the patent literature
works.abstract: The patent literature is a major source of scientific and technical information for drug discovery, often disclosing chemical structures, biological targets, therapeutic indications, and structure-activity relationships before they appear in the scientific literature. However, patent documents are difficult to analyse at scale because of their volume, legal and technical language, heterogeneous formats, and frequent use of nonmachine-readable representations for chemical structures. Since 2015, SureChEMBL has provided open access to chemical information automatically extracted from patent documents. Here, we present a major redesign of the SureChEMBL resource. The updated platform is built on a modern architecture and includes redesigned extraction, chemistry registration, search and data-delivery workflows, together with large-scale reprocessing of the historical corpus through a unified standardization pipeline. SureChEMBL also introduces automatically generated biomedical annotations for genes, proteins, diseases, and mechanisms, linking patent chemistry to biological context. The resource currently contains 122 million patents, 44 million chemically annotated documents, 31 million chemical structures, and 1 million biomedical entity annotations, accessible through https://www.surechembl.org/, an API and the downloadable Bulk Data.

works.title: OmniVira: a knowledgebase of source-linked evidence on viral spillover and cross-species transmission
works.abstract: Zoonotic viral emergence poses persistent challenges to global health, yet evidence relevant to spillover and cross-species transmission is dispersed across surveillance, epidemiological, experimental, mechanistic, and genomic studies. Here, we present OmniVira (https://omnivira.org/), a curated knowledgebase that transforms literature-derived findings into structured, traceable, and reusable OmniVira Evidence (OVE) records. OmniVira implements an auditable article-evidence framework linking individual findings and supporting text to normalized virus, host, and geographic entities, and relevant biological context. A domain-specific ontology organizes 14 evidence types into five categories: Zoonotic Surveillance, Transmission Evidence, Experimental Infection, Functional Mechanism, and Genomic Evolution. The platform integrates ontology-guided curation, large language model-assisted literature screening and candidate extraction, automated consistency checks, and curator review of flagged or ambiguous records, enabling daily updates. As of 4 August 2026, OmniVira contained 8072 publicly retrievable OVE records derived from 2623 source articles, spanning 60 ICTV virus families, 55 host orders, and 121 countries. Its responsive interface supports evidence-centred retrieval, source-text verification, and exploration of linked virus-host-literature relationships across desktop and mobile browsers. OmniVira provides a transparent, context-preserving resource for systematic comparison and synthesis of evidence related to zoonotic viral emergence and cross-species transmission.

works.title: PED in 2027: integrating experimental and predicted protein conformational ensembles at scale
works.abstract: The Protein Ensemble Database (PED; https://proteinensemble.org) is the primary deposition resource for structural ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). PED 2027 (released in September 2026) substantially expands its scope by integrating ensembles determined or refined using experimental data with clearly identified collections of computational predictions. The release introduces a multi-method collection targeting 3319 DisProt proteins and 2452 manually curated disordered regions, together with AlphaFlex ensembles for 10 022 human proteins containing IDRs. Alternative predictions for the same sequence are retained as independent records with method-specific provenance, enabling comparison across ensemble-generation approaches. A scalable deposition workflow accommodates individual experimental studies and proteome-scale collections while preserving quality control and curator oversight. The PED controlled vocabulary standardizes experimental data acquisition, computational generation, selection, and refinement. Precomputed IDPEnsembleTools and CIDER analyses provide structural and sequence-derived descriptors directly on ensemble pages. A redesigned interface and extended REST API support discovery, visualization, download and programmatic access. Interoperability with UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, and experimental-data repositories connects ensembles with sequences, annotations, and supporting measurements. PED 2027 therefore provides an interoperable, analysis-ready platform for studying IDP/IDR conformational behaviour.

works.title: Omni-ARMD: an integrated genomic and clinical knowledgebase bridging clinical phenotypes and molecular determinants of antimicrobial resistance
works.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, yet its molecular determinants remain difficult to characterize in real-world settings, as genomic and clinical data are fragmented across resources. Existing databases typically separate gene-level mechanisms, curated genotype-phenotype associations, and large-scale clinical antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) data, limiting cross-scale interpretation. Here, we present Omni-ARMD, an open-access knowledgebase that integrates multi-source genomic and clinical data to systematically infer genotype-phenotype relationships in AMR. Omni-ARMD bridges large-scale clinical AST records and gene-level resistance evidence through a confidence-weighted log-odds enrichment framework, which quantifies genotype-phenotype associations at the organism-antimicrobial level and integrates these associations into aggregated cross-domain evidence representations. The current release includes over 12 million de-identified microbiology records from more than 1 million patients, harmonized to generate over 7.83 million standardized AST records. It also integrates over 0.36 million gene-phenotype associations, spanning 38 organisms, 52 antimicrobials, and 375 resistance genes. Omni-ARMD links over 5.16 million clinical records to genomic evidence, achieving a 65.86% match rate and a 2.61% coverage of organism-antimicrobial pairs. Omni-ARMD provides interactive modules for clinical investigation, genomic evidence analysis, mechanistic interpretation, and artificial intelligence-assisted exploration, enabling integrative and data-driven discovery in AMR. Omni-ARMD is freely available at www.omniarmd.cn.

works.title: Root endophyte sulfur metabolites enhance redox balance and drought tolerance in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: Drought is a major consequence of climate change and significantly limits crop productivity. Plant growth-promoting bacteria offer a promising solution to mitigate drought stress. The root endophyte Pseudomonas argentinensis SA190 has been shown to enhance plant performance under drought stress conditions, but the mechanistic basis of SA190's beneficial effects remained unclear. Given the pivotal role of sulfur-containing compounds in abiotic stress responses, we investigated multiple sulfur-related Arabidopsis mutants under PEG-induced drought stress. We found that SA190 enhances sulfate uptake and promotes glutathione (GSH) accumulation in shoots under stress conditions. SA190 treatment increased the GSH/GSSG ratio, providing an enhanced redox resilience under PEG stress. Inhibition of GSH biosynthesis in Arabidopsis with buthionine sulfoximine (BSO) provided evidence that SA190 contributes to elevated GSH levels under PEG-induced drought stress. Using bacterial mutants defective in GSH biosynthesis, we further show that SA190 contributes to Arabidopsis growth under PEG-induced stress, potentially through a mechanism involving bacterial GSH itself or its precursor, γ -glutamylcysteine (γ-EC). In summary, SA190 enhances tolerance to PEG-induced drought stress by modulating host sulfur metabolism and improving cellular redox homeostasis.

works.title: Seven ways not to think carefully about aging
works.abstract: Many experts in the field of biogerontology organize their research plans based on conceptual schemas that are hard to justify, logically problematic, and distracting. These include the ideas: (a) that there is a cause for aging; (b) that each person has a biological age; (c) that published clocks can measure that biological age; (d) that cells have an age; (e) that old cells can rejuvenate and become young again; (f) that biomarkers of age measure rate of aging; (g) that interventions improve either healthspan or lifespan, but not both; and (h) that collections of Hallmarks of aging move the field forward, not backwards. Recognizing the problems and inconsistencies of these very common (though often unconscious) assumptions could help scientists think more clearly and effectively about what to work on. Accumulating data from mouse studies suggest that many or all varieties of slow-aging, long-lived mice, even as young adults, share multiple physiological and molecular traits whose effects may shed light on the pathogenesis of late-life disease, and whose origins may point to new anti-aging interventions. This Comment critiques assumptions and paradigms frequently used in the geroscience field, aiming at enhancing clarity and plausibility of research and conceptual frameworks within and beyond the aging community.

works.title: CDH1 loss remodels gene expression and lineage identity in human mammary epithelial cells
works.abstract: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is a common subtype of breast cancer, molecularly defined by genetic loss of CDH1, and subsequent loss of cell adhesion protein E-cadherin, in ~95% of ILC. Though CDH1 loss occurs early in ILC oncogenesis, it is unclear how this facilitates transformation. We modeled early CDH1 loss using "normal" human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC), i.e., finite lifespan cells reflecting early hyperplasia, and targeted E-cadherin signaling using antibodies versus causing genetic CDH1 loss using siRNA or CRISPR/Cas9-knockout. Transcriptome analysis across four HMEC models showed that the mode of E-cadherin targeting is critical for the subsequent phenotype. Antibody-mediated inhibition of cell-cell contacts induced gene signatures of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), consistent with the role of E-cadherin suppression during the EMT process. Conversely, genetic CDH1 loss - as in ILC oncogenesis - repressed EMT signatures, and instead remodeled gene expression toward a luminal epithelial phenotype. RNA-seq, single cell transcriptomics, flow cytometry, microscopy, and ATAC-seq analyses support that CDH1 loss induces lineage remodeling to a luminal state, which is mirrored in transcriptomic analysis of clinical ILC precursor lesions. By isolating luminal versus basal cells prior to CDH1 knockout, we found that CDH1 loss led to remodeling of lineage identity in both populations, converging on a new lineage homeostasis with a luminal progenitor-like phenotype. Consistent with the shift to a luminal progenitor phenotype, CDH1 loss enhanced proliferative capacity over the finite lifespan of the HMECs, highlighting a feature of early CDH1 loss that may contribute to clonal advantage during tumor initiation. Moreover, CDH1 loss enhanced anoikis resistance, a defining feature of ILC cells. Our findings support that genetic loss of CDH1 in mammary epithelial cells induces transcriptional and phenotypic changes consistent with lineage identity remodeling toward a luminal progenitor-like state, which may underpin the mechanism by which early CDH1 loss mediates ILC oncogenesis.

works.title: The peculiar properties of pericentromeric regions of genomes and their influence on sex chromosome evolution
works.abstract: Results from recent genome sequences support the idea that the lack of recombination across extensive sex-linked regions (SLRs) in some species may be a pre-existing feature, due mainly to the sex-determining locus being located near a centromere. This would cause it to be affected by the "centromere-effect", which ensures low recombination rates near centromeres. In such cases, it is unnecessary to invoke any active recombination suppression process, or to debate ideas about the types of selection involved. In this review, I outline the properties of genome regions that recombine rarely, including pericentromeric regions of chromosomes, and discuss SLRs that overlap with pericentromeric regions. Unsurprisingly, it is difficult to distinguish special features of such SLRs that would suggest they have undergone a recombination suppression process. The property most likely to be specific to completely SLRs is major gene loss from Y- or W-linked regions of genes found in their respective X- or Z-linked counterparts, and this asymmetry is observed in many species. However, if pericentromeric regions are characterised by ephemeral gene content and low gene expression, asymmetry between pericentromeric SLRs might be less pronounced than in SLRs in other genome regions, and similar Y and X degeneration levels are indeed documented in several species. Additionally, some such SLRs may not be completely sex-linked, which could explain findings of extensive SLRs with low Y-X (or W-Z) divergence.

works.title: Polygenic adaptation signals reveal selection on key behavioral traits early in dog domestication history
works.abstract: Dogs, the first domesticated animals, show behavioral and morphological changes shaped by artificial selection, but when and where these traits were selected remains unclear. Analyzing two independent canine genomic datasets comprising 1,987 and 722 individuals, we found that polygenic shifts in key behavioral traits associated with domestication were more consistently shared across dog lineages than those in morphological traits. Specifically, we first grouped breeds into three major genetic lineages-Asian Spitz, African-Middle Eastern, and European Modern-and integrated genomic variation with breed-level measures of 36 behavioral and four morphological traits. We then tested polygenic adaptation using pairwise population comparisons and PolyGraph. Across both datasets, pro-social behavioral shifts, particularly reduced owner-directed aggression and non-social fear, showed the most consistent selection signals. PolyGraph detected shifts toward lower values for both traits on branches ancestral to the major dog lineages. Trainability showed an ancestral increase, whereas attachment/attention seeking increased in specific lineages, based on dog-only analyses designed to minimize rearing-related confounding in wolves. Hunting-related behaviors also showed lineage-specific shifts, while morphological traits varied substantially across datasets and lineages. Ancient genetic trait scores mirrored these patterns: prehistoric dogs already differed from wolves in shared pro-social behavioral traits and displayed lineage-specific shifts in hunting-related behaviors, whereas morphological scores remained heterogeneous. Together, these findings indicate that both shared behavioral changes and functional differentiation among dog lineages began early in domestication.

works.title: Metazoan Orc6 proteins evolved alternative mechanisms for association with the ORC complex: insights from Drosophila modeling
works.abstract: In eukaryotes, DNA replication requires the origin recognition complex (ORC), a six-subunit assembly that promotes replisome formation on chromosomal origins. Orc6 is the smallest and least evolutionarily conserved among all ORC subunits. In Drosophila, Orc6 binds tightly with the core ORC(1-5) and is required for DNA binding and replication initiation, whereas in Xenopus and human systems Orc6 loosely associates with the rest of the complex resulting in some differences for replication-associated activities. Despite these variations, Orc6 remains essential for viability in all species. In current study we analyzed specific residues within the C-terminal α11 helix that is critical for stable association of Orc6 with the ORC complex in Drosophila. Human Orc6 lacks these residues, however it possesses a strong nuclear localization signal (NLS) that is absent in Drosophilidae. We propose that this NLS drives human protein to the nucleus and compensates for weaker Orc6-ORC(1-5) interactions by increasing the nuclear concentration of Orc6 and shifting the equilibrium toward formation of the fully assembled ORC complex at the DNA.

works.title: Diverse RNA Editing Systems Across Heterolobosea (Discoba)
works.abstract: Mitochondrial RNA editing events were previously reported in only three unrelated species within the phylum Heterolobosea (Discoba): Naegleria gruberi and Acrasis kona (which performs C-to-U substitutions) and Pharyngomonadida sp. BB2 (which inserts single nucleotides by a yet unknown mechanism). We present novel high-quality genome assemblies obtained via a combination of whole-genome and targeted sequencing approaches and predicted proteomes for two species, Paravahlkampfia ustiana and Heteramoeba clara, representing an understudied clade of the phylum. Surprisingly, we discovered RNA editing events of C-to-U substitutions and mononucleotide insertions co-existing in the mitochondria of P. ustiana, while the two systems were both absent in H. clara. In addition, P. ustiana also exhibits A-to-I editing sites in rRNA transcripts encoded in multicopy circular rDNA plasmids. RNA editing events in P. ustiana were verified by proteomics, Illumina short RNA reads, ONT long cDNA and direct RNA reads. We elaborate on the potential mechanisms of mitochondrial insertional editing by investigating several aspects of the RNA transcription machinery and base modifications in template DNA and mRNA products. We report additional cases of C-to-U RNA editing in other species of Heterolobosea and explore the distribution of various putative components of the C-to-U editosome, including the DYW domain-containing pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, across the phylum expanding the understanding of the evolutionary dynamics underlying this phenomenon, which remains understudied outside land plants. The comparative analysis of available sequence data from Heterolobosea revealed that C-to-U RNA editing was acquired relatively deep in the evolution of Heterolobosea and subsequently underwent repeated losses.

works.title: Using SpliceAI to triage splice-altering variants in 7,220 individuals with rare conditions highlights limitations of the precomputed scores
works.abstract: Abstract Background SpliceAI is a deep learning algorithm that predicts whether genetic variants are likely to affect splicing. Precomputed SpliceAI predictions for all theoretical SNVs and small indels were released in 2019, and are used by variant annotation tools such as VEP and dbNSFP to batch annotate large numbers of variants quickly. While the use of precomputed scores vastly reduces the computational cost of retrieving SpliceAI predictions, several limitations to their utility have emerged, for which the impact on the prioritisation of likely splice-altering variants in cohort studies has not been established. Methods We identify transcript annotation and genome version inconsistencies impacting the precomputed SpliceAI scores by comparing the original gene annotation file with MANE v1.0 Select transcripts. To quantify the impact that these factors may have in variant prioritisation pipelines for diagnostic purposes, we re-analysed variants in 660 genes linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), identified in 7,221 participants with NDD from the Genomics England 100,000 Genomes Project (100kGP). Results We find outdated gene annotations and genome version inconsistencies impact 8.34% of theoretical SNVs included in the SpliceAI precomputed scores, and affect the accuracy of SpliceAI predictions in 34.98% of disease-associated panelApp green genes. In 7,221 Genomics England participants, re-running SpliceAI with updated annotations and parameters results in an increase of 18.2% predicted splice-altering variants compared with variants identified using precomputed scores alone. These variants constitute a diagnostic increase of 11.7% versus the precomputed scores, assessed retrospectively using confirmed diagnoses in 100kGP. To mitigate issues with the precomputed scores we provide ‘SpliceAI-splint’- a command-line tool to allow users to identify variants within a VCF file whose potential splice-altering effects would be missed by the precomputed scores. Conclusions: Although the precomputed scores continue to represent a useful resource in the annotation of variants in cohorts with genetic disorders, we find key limitations that can lead to their missing clinically relevant splice-altering variants, and provide a command-line tool to mitigate these issues.

works.title: Ciprofloxacin resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae: phenotype prediction from genotype and global distribution of resistance determinants
authors: Emília Maria Medeiros de Andrade Belitardo
works.abstract: Abstract Background Ciprofloxacin resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is common or emerging in many geographies, and knowledge of local resistance rates is important for empirical therapy. While K. pneumoniae ciprofloxacin resistance determinants are known, there is a lack of systematic data on the effect of these determinants, alone and in combination, and there are no publicly accessible tools for predicting ciprofloxacin resistance from whole genome sequence data. Methods The KlebNET-GSP AMR Genotype-Phenotype Group aggregated a matched genotype-phenotype dataset of n = 12,167 K. pneumoniae species complex ( Kp SC) isolates from 27 countries between 2001 and 2021. We developed a rule-based classifier to predict ciprofloxacin resistance by categorizing the number of mutations in the quinolone resistance determining regions of gyrA and parC and the number of plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance genes, including the presence/absence of aac(6 ' )-Ib-cr (which can acetylate ciprofloxacin). Predictive performance was assessed using the discovery dataset, with the reassessment of discrepant and concordant isolates; and validated using externally contributed datasets ( n = 7,030 Kp SC isolates). Results The rule-based classifier predicted R vs S/I with categorical agreement, sensitivity, and specificity > 96%, and major/very major error rates < 4%. Performance was similar across diverse Kp SC sources (human, animal, other), species, and intra-species lineages. External validation of the classifier yielded overall 90.18% categorical agreement [95% confidence interval (CI), 89.49–90.88%], 8.74% major errors [95% CI, 7.41–10.06%], 4.19% very major errors [95% CI, 3.60–4.77%], and 10.14% minor errors [95% CI, 9.44–10.85%]. We implemented the classifier in Kleborate, a command-line tool that is integrated into the Pathogenwatch web platform. Using this to assess the global distribution of ciprofloxacin resistance determinants in Kp SC genomes available in Pathogenwatch ( n = 31,319, from 109 countries between years 2000–2023), we observed a significant positive association between national quinolone consumption rates and predicted ciprofloxacin resistance (R 2 = 0.20, p = 0.004). Conclusion Ciprofloxacin resistance phenotypes can be reasonably predicted from genotype, which is sufficient for informing surveillance. However, unexplained resistance remains and accuracy is insufficient for clinical applications. We demonstrate the value of aggregating genotype-phenotype data to explore resistance mechanisms and develop predictors, but highlight complexities in combining phenotype data from different assays and standards.

works.title: Germline pathogenic variants identification through comprehensive cancer genome profiling
works.abstract: Comprehensive cancer genome profiling (CGP) is recommended for the identification of actionable somatic mutations in a selected subgroup of cancer patients. Some variants detected by CGP can be constitutional. The aim of this study is to evaluate the rate of potential and confirmed constitutional pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants (overall defined as PVs) identified through CGP according to the recommendations of the European Society of Medical Oncology. This is a prospective interventional trial that enrolled patients with solid cancers in whom molecular assessment was clinically indicated based on national guidelines, referring them for CGP (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06020625). Patients with suspected constitutional variants were subsequently referred for germline testing. The present analysis focuses on the first two years of the program, from January 2022 to December 2023. Of 2688 samples (2674 patients) with a CGP report, more than half were represented by gynecologic cancers (endometrial and ovarian). 16% of the patients were addressed to genetic evaluation for 527 suspected constitutional PVs, with a compliance to genetic counselling of 80%. 331 patients underwent germline testing, of whom 73% harbored at least one PV, with 66% of tested variants confirmed to be germline. Interestingly, 16% of germline variants were secondary findings and 20% of the confirmed “on-tumor” germline PVs were in moderate-risk genes. Twenty additional constitutional PVs were identified in 19 patients based on the results of other somatic tests or through additional tests requested following genetic counselling (0.7% of the entire cohort). Constitutional PVs were detected in about 10% of an unselected solid tumor cohort through CGP. A relevant fraction of the constitutional PVs were secondary findings or constitutional variants in moderate penetrance genes, that would not have been detected based on current guidelines. The integration of CGP with systematic genetic counseling provides a comprehensive approach that optimizes both therapeutic decision-making and identification of hereditary cancer syndromes. Protocol ID: FPG500, ID number: 3837. The study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06020625.

works.title: Comprehensive adjudication identifies 108 high-confidence genetic signals for Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias
works.abstract: The Alzheimer’s Disease Sequencing Project Gene Verification Committee developed and applied a systematic framework to adjudicate genetic evidence for AD and related dementias, addressing wide variation in association quality. Phase 1 established tiered criteria by evaluating 23 nominated loci across study designs. Phase 2 applied this framework to 29 large-scale genome-wide studies published between January 2015 and September 2022 (date of the last literature search), tiering 163 unique loci. Phase 1 yielded 17 high-confidence association signals, including 12 with specific gene-level support. Phase 2 identified 93 high-confidence single-variant signals and 25 high-confidence variant-set signals. After removal of overlapping signals across evidence classes, a final catalog of 108 unique high-confidence AD/ADRD-associated signals were generated. Prioritized loci highlight APP processing, microglial immunity, and lipid metabolism pathways, including genes not captured by existing resources like Agora or Open Targets. Summarized results can be viewed at https://topgenes.niagads.org/ . This rigorously adjudicated catalog represents the most comprehensive AD/ADRD genetics resource to date, providing a foundation for functional validation and therapeutic discovery with broad applicability to complex diseases.

works.title: Resolving disease causality by integrating polygenic risk into propensity score matching
works.abstract: Disentangling causal relationships between diseases from associations driven by shared genetic and environmental risk remains a major challenge. We developed PRIMA (polygenic risk–integrated matching approach), a framework that incorporates exposure-specific polygenic risk scores and clinical covariates into propensity score matching. We evaluated PRIMA using liability-threshold simulations and disease-pair analyses in 333,370 unrelated UK Biobank participants of European ancestry, and compared its estimates with clinical matching, Mendelian randomization and survival analyses. In simulations, PRIMA reduced bias due to shared genetic liability and recovered effect estimates closer to the expected causal effects than clinical matching alone, while remaining sensitive to unmeasured confounding. In UK Biobank analyses, integrating polygenic risk improved genetic and clinical balance and materially altered association estimates for a subset of disease pairs. PRIMA identified additional associations not detected by Mendelian randomization and showed greater concordance with survival analyses. PRIMA provides a scalable framework for incorporating polygenic liability into observational disease-pair analyses. It complements existing causal inference methods, although causal interpretation remains conditional on appropriate model specification, sufficient overlap and adequate control of confounding.

works.title: Tracing the origins of multidrug resistant bacteria in Ukraine
works.abstract: Abstract Background A key medical characteristic of the current conflict in Ukraine has been the extraordinary number of wounds being infected by multidrug resistant organisms (MDROs). The origin and spread of these organisms have been the subject of intense interest and debate, yet the reservoirs and transmission routes remain poorly defined. In this study, environmental sampling was performed across the Ukrainian medical evacuation chain to better understand transmission dynamics. Methods 127 environmental swabs were collected from environmental surfaces in three frontline hospitals ( n = 17 swabs), two evacuation assets (12 swabs), a large regional healthcare facility that provides full clinical and surgical capabilities (23 swabs), and three definitive care and rehabilitative hospitals (75 swabs). Swabs were incubated in Brain Heart Infusion broth and then cultured on non-selective and selective agars. Short- and long-read sequencing were performed using an Illumina NextSeq 2000 and MinION, respectively. The resulting genomes were compared to a collection of clinical bacteria cultured from patients in healthcare facilities in Denmark, Germany, The Netherlands, and Ukraine. Results Bacterial growth was recorded from 112 swabs (88%) and 280 distinct environmental strains, representing 89 bacterial species, were cultured. Notably, MDROs were effectively absent from the frontline facilitates and evacuation assets but were detected in 48–56% of environmental samples from rear-echelon hospitals. Genomic analysis revealed that these rear-echelon hospital environments were dominated by epidemic lineages of Acinetobacter baumannii , Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and Klebsiella pneumoniae that frequently carried carbapenemases. A genetic comparison of the environmental bacteria with clinical strains cultured from injured soldiers and refugees receiving care in hospitals in Ukraine, Denmark, Germany, and The Netherlands revealed high levels of genetic relatedness. Compounding the problem, plasmidome analysis identified horizontal dissemination of resistance genes across species within the hospital environment. Conclusions These findings implicate hospital environments as key reservoirs and amplifiers of MDROs during conflict, highlighting their central role in sustaining local transmission and international spread.

works.title: Evaluating gene expression-based approaches for functional assessment of non-coding variants in neurodevelopmental disorders
works.abstract: Non-coding variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders are difficult to interpret because their regulatory effects are subtle and depend on locus- and stage-specific epigenetic contexts. Transcriptional mis-regulation of nearby genes is the most reliable sign of functional relevance. RNA-seq studies usually detect this via differential gene expression (DEG) analysis, which requires healthy controls and typically more than twofold expression changes. Allele-specific expression (ASE) analysis, may detect subtler effects by directly comparing expression of alleles on the intact and the affected chromosomes within the same sample. We evaluated ASE power using real RNA-seq data, in silico simulations, and a clinical case. We combined transcriptome profiling of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and neural progenitor cells (NPCs) with in silico modeling of gene-expression changes to estimate statistical power. We compared two strategies: DEG between variant carriers and non-carriers, and ASE within heterozygous individuals. For clinical validation, we used CRISPR-Cas9 base editing to introduce a synonymous single-nucleotide variant (SNV) adjacent to the candidate regulatory variant in patient-derived NPCs and performed targeted RNA-seq. Simulations and empirical data showed that DEG has higher power for most genes, even with substantial inter-individual or biological variability. ASE surpassed DEG only for genes containing heterozygous SNVs and sequenced at high depth. In a patient carrying a translocation breakpoint near AUTS2 , we generated iPSC and NPC lines with SNV-labeled AUTS2 alleles and devised an inexpensive target-enrichment assay for high-sensitivity ASE profiling, but neither approach detected gene misregulation consistent with the phenotype under current biological models. Our results suggested that DEG and ASE assays are complementary rather than competing strategies. We also demonstrate a practical path to sensitive ASE detection, both in whole-transcriptome and targeted RNA-sequencing, using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated allele labeling. This framework helps researchers to choose cost-effective transcriptomic designs for the functional validation of non-coding variants implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders.

works.title: Pilot Evaluation of Saliva Samples as An Alternative to Blood for Large-scale Whole-genome Sequencing Studies
works.abstract: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) studies have traditionally relied on blood as the primary DNA source and manual workflows. As population-based genomics studies expand, minimally invasive and easily deployable biospecimen collection methods compatible with high-throughput automation are increasingly needed. In this pilot study, we established a real-world, end-to-end automated WGS workflow, encompassing robotic DNA extraction, library preparation, sequencing and quality control. We compared saliva- and blood-derived WGS across key analytical parameters, including performance at each step of the workflow, overall cost, and feasibility for future large-scale implementation. First, germline variant calls from saliva and blood samples showed high concordance, reaching 97% genome-wide and over 99% in high-confidence genomic regions. Second, key workflow metrics, including DNA quality and sequencing quality, were comparable between saliva and blood samples, while saliva samples had a lower per-sample cost. We compared three commercially available saliva collection kits and found that all achieved at least 95% genome-wide concordance with matched blood samples, with differences primarily driven by cost. Finally, automated saliva processing produced sequencing and short variant calling metrics broadly comparable to manual processing in a small paired comparison. Collectively, these results provide a practical and scalable solution for incorporating saliva into future large cohort sequencing studies. Larger and more diverse studies are needed to further validate the robustness and generalizability of this pilot study.

works.title: Quantification method affects replicability of eQTL analysis, colocalization and TWAS
Interferon-α directs hematopoietic stem cells toward competing fates
fastGxE is a powerful method for uncovering genotype–environment interactions in biobanks
How the TREX-2 complex associates with the nuclear pore
works.abstract: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) control nucleocytoplasmic transport in eukaryotes, yet their architecture remains incompletely understood. Here, we report a substantially extended structure of the human NPC, obtained by combining cryo-electron tomography, crosslinking mass spectrometry, and AI-assisted integrative modeling. We resolve the molecular arrangement of translocated promoter region (TPR), NUP153, NUP50, and ZC3HC1 and reveal that five additional proteins-TMEM209, SMPD4, GANP, Centrin-2, and ENY2-are incorporated into the NPC. Unexpectedly, GANP, Centrin-2, and ENY2, core members of the TREX-2 mRNA export complex, are built into the nuclear ring. This finding establishes TREX-2 not as a transiently associated factor, but as an integral NPC module, positioning it opposite of the cytoplasmic NUP214 mRNA export platform. Together, our results redefine the molecular composition of the inner ring, nuclear ring, and nuclear basket. They suggest a direct structural basis that couples TREX-2-mediated messenger ribonucleoprotein particle (mRNP) remodeling to NPC-facilitated transport.

works.title: Small genomes, big lessons: What viruses teach us about structure-based riboregulation
works.abstract: RNA viruses encode multiple layers of information within a single molecule, which functions simultaneously as a template for protein synthesis and as a structured regulatory RNA. These structures control key aspects of viral gene expression, govern host interactions, and mediate immune evasion. Although the prevalence of RNA structure in viral genomes is now well established, only recently have functional and mechanistic studies begun to uncover how these elements act as regulatory modules that shape infection outcomes. With their compact genomes and experimentally tractable life cycles, RNA viruses represent powerful model systems for uncovering the fundamental building blocks of riboregulation and illuminating principles of gene control conserved across eukaryotes. Here, we review current mechanistic understanding of RNA structure-based regulation across diverse viral families and draw parallels to structure-mediated gene control in eukaryotic transcriptomes, highlighting RNA structure as a central regulatory layer in gene expression with broad therapeutic and synthetic biology potential.

works.title: A phage-encoded GapR nucleoid-associated protein binds a bacterial GapR to deactivate it via an inhibitory hetero-oligomer mechanism
works.abstract: Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in bacterial chromosome organization and cellular processes. Recent work identified GapR as an essential NAP that is ubiquitous in α-proteobacteria. GapR structures revealed that the GapR dimer can form dimer of dimers in the presence of DNA to create a DNA-encasing clamp and data showed that GapR is required for bacterial replication as it recruits topoisomerases to regions of overtwisted DNA. Interestingly, diverse phages that infect α-proteobacteria encode GapR homologs. To gain insight into how phage GapRs may impact their cellular homologs we performed structure/function analyses on the Roseobacterial and Roseophage RDJLΦ1 GapR proteins. Crystal structures revealed that the RDJLΦ1 GapR structure differs from that of the bacterial GapR in a way that is incompatible with DNA binding. Cellular localization and fluorescence binding assays confirmed that the RDJLΦ1 phage GapR does not bind DNA. Strikingly, we show that the RDJLΦ1 GapR and Roseobacterial GapR can form heterodimers that are unable to bind DNA, suggesting the phage GapR may act as a bacterial GapR poison. This was further supported by cellular studies. Collectively these studies reveal a unique autoinhibitory mechanism by which a phage encoded NAP impacts DNA binding by the host NAP.

works.title: Molecular mechanisms of the Asx C-terminal region for genomic targeting of PR-DUB in Drosophila
works.abstract: Polycomb-repressive deubiquitinase (PR-DUB) removes monoubiquitin from histone H2A at lysine 119 in mammals and lysine 118 in Drosophila (H2Aub1). This reaction requires interaction of the PR-DUB catalytic subunit Bap1 with the N terminus of its partner Asx. In Drosophila , Asx truncation mutants lacking the C-terminal low-complexity region and PHD finger display severe PR-DUB loss-of-function phenotypes. PR-DUB containing C-terminally truncated Asx retains deubiquitinase activity but fails to localize to Polycomb target genes, resulting in excessive H2Aub1 accumulation that disrupts repression. Unexpectedly, the conserved interaction between the Asx PHD finger and Mbd5 is dispensable for viability but fine-tunes H2Aub1 deubiquitination at a subset of Polycomb target genes. In contrast, a short domain in the Asx C terminus that associates with the DNA-binding domain of the Polycomb protein Pho is essential for viability. The Asx–Pho interaction is required for recruitment of PR-DUB to most Polycomb target genes, where it promotes H2Aub1 deubiquitination and preserves Polycomb repression. Unlike the widely conserved PHD finger, the Pho-interacting motif in Asx is conserved only across arthropods. The Asx C terminus therefore constitutes a modular interaction platform in which conserved protein interactions modulate PR-DUB activity, whereas evolutionarily restricted interactions direct its genomic targeting.

works.title: Integration-free and cluster-free detection of localized differential gene coexpression in single-cell data with DiCoLo
works.abstract: Detecting changes in gene coordination patterns between biological conditions and identifying the cell populations in which these changes occur are key challenges in single-cell analysis. Existing approaches often compare gene co-expression between predefined cell clusters or rely on aligning cells across conditions. These strategies can be suboptimal when changes occur within small subpopulations or when batch effects obscure the underlying biological signal. To address these challenges, we introduce DiCoLo, a framework that identifies genes exhibiting differential co-localization, defined as changes in coordinated expression within localized cell neighborhoods -subsets of highly similar cells in the transcriptomic space. Importantly, DiCoLo does not rely on cell clustering or cross-condition alignment. For each condition, DiCoLo constructs a gene graph using Optimal Transport distances that reflect gene co-localization patterns across the cell manifold. Then, it identifies differential gene programs by detecting changes in connectivity patterns between the gene graphs. We show that DiCoLo robustly identifies differential gene co-localization even under weak signals or complex batch effects, outperforming existing methods across multiple benchmark datasets. When applied to mouse hair follicle development data, DiCoLo reveals coordinated gene programs and emerging cell populations driven by perturbations in morphogen signaling that underlie dermal condensate differentiation. Overall, these results establish DiCoLo as a powerful framework for uncovering localized differential transcriptional coordinated patterns in single-cell data.

works.title: Chromosome-scale genome assembly and annotation of Octodon degus
works.abstract: Abstract High-quality reference genomes are essential for comparative and functional genomics yet remain unavailable for many emerging model organisms. Here, we report OctDeg2.0, a chromosome-level genome assembly and annotation of the degu ( Octodon degus), generated using PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing and Hi-C scaffolding from a single male individual. Octodon degus is of growing interest as a natural animal model for aging and Alzheimer’s disease research. The 3.4 billion base-pair assembly comprises 28 autosomes and both sex chromosomes, with markedly improved contiguity and completeness over the prior short-read assembly while maintaining high base accuracy. The new assembly provides substantially enhanced gene annotation, clearer resolution of chromatin architecture and cis-regulatory element landscapes, with much improved characterization of repetitive and structurally complex regions, including centromeres and segmental duplications. We present a streamlined and reproducible pipeline for high-resolution de novo genome assembly and gene annotation applicable to other emerging model organisms. This work establishes a robust genomic resource for studying molecular and cellular mechanisms in health and disease in Octodon degus .

works.title: Sequence design for three-dimensional genome folding using Akita Semifreddo
works.abstract: DNA sequence directs genome folding, which in turn shapes enhancer-promoter communication and gene expression. How to design DNA sequences that produce desired folding patterns remains largely unexplored. Here we present Akita Semifreddo, which combines an efficient "half-frozen" version of the AkitaV2 genome folding model with the Ledidi sequence optimizer to design DNA sequences with desired folding in silico. We demonstrate that this framework enables design for major folding features – boundaries, dots, and flames – with desired positions and strengths. In short, Akita Semifreddo provides a platform for dissecting the sequence grammar of genome folding and engineering synthetic regulatory landscapes.

works.title: ReadsRatio: a facile method for cell type deconvolution with cross-platform applications
works.abstract: Existing methylation-based cfDNA deconvolution methods are sensitive to sequencing depth, reference quality, and platform variability. We develope ReadsRatio, an approach to estimate tissue proportions using the ratio of unmethylated reads within cell type-specific marker regions, without requiring reference methylation intensity signals. Compared to conventional methods, ReadsRatio detects specific tissue involvement in both simulations and clinical cohorts involving lupus, kidney transplantation, and COVID-19. It maintains accuracy across sequencing platforms and at reduced sequencing depths, enabling substantial cost savings in our preliminary estimations. ReadsRatio provides a versatile, cost-efficient framework for cfDNA deconvolution with broad research and clinical applicability.

works.title: Urbanisation drives parallel genomic divergence across cities and bumble bee species
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Urbanisation imposes pervasive environmental change, yet it remains unclear whether evolutionary responses to cities are largely idiosyncratic or whether similar selective pressures across cities repeatedly generate predictable genomic outcomes. RESULTS: Here, we analyse whole-genome data from 524 individuals of three widespread bumble bee species sampled across nine independent urban-rural pairs in Central Europe to test whether urban environments drive parallel evolutionary responses across cities and species. Genetic diversity responded idiosyncratically to urbanisation, with two species showing no detectable urban-rural differences and one species exhibiting reduced diversity in cities, consistent with species-specific ecological traits and habitat requirements. Despite weak population structure and high gene flow in all species, we detected consistent and replicated genomic divergence associated with urban environments. Genome-environment association analyses revealed parallel allele-frequency shifts at the same loci across independent cities for each species, while selective sweep scans identified repeated signals of positive selection in urban populations. Across species, urban-associated divergence was highly polygenic and occurred predominantly in non-coding regions with potential regulatory roles. Although the specific genes involved were largely species-specific, functional enrichment analyses revealed strong convergence across species, particularly in pathways related to physiological stress responses, neurocognitive and behavioural processes, metabolism and immunity. CONCLUSIONS: Together, these results suggest that urban environments can impose recurrent selective pressures, generating predictable and parallel genomic responses across cities and species despite ongoing gene flow. More broadly, our findings highlight polygenic, potentially regulatory adaptation as an important component of evolutionary responses to urban environments.

works.title: Mitonuclear control of transcription complexes regulates tRNA splicing
works.abstract: The human genome has hundreds of tRNA genes, a subset of which is intervened by short introns. Transcription of the latter genes by RNA polymerase (Pol) III generates precursor tRNAs that undergo splicing by the tRNA splicing complex, in addition to the removal of flanking sequences by RNase P and RNase Z. The former enzyme consists of tRNA splicing endoribonuclease complex and tRNA ligase complex. However, it was unknown how and where the human tRNA splicing complex executes its function in cells. We show that transcription complexes assembled on intron-containing tRNA genes possess a tRNA ligase complex and that this enzyme is regulated by a mitonuclear communication mechanism. A cytoplasmic, mitochondria-associated HSPC117, the catalytic subunit of the tRNA ligase complex, transiently relocates to the nucleoplasm in the S phase of the cell cycle to promote the second step of splicing, exon ligation, of select tRNAs. This nuclear localized RTCB-type ligase acts as an integral part of transcription complexes. Knockout of HSPC117 or expression of an inactive mutant of this enzyme leads to severe inhibition of transcription and exon ligation due to the assembly of deficient transcription complexes. Inhibition also brings to deficiency of the perinucleolar compartments, as a result of reduced expression of the H1 RNA essential to Pol III transcription in cells. This study demonstrates that transcription complexes execute splicing of select intron-containing tRNAs and that this two-stage reaction is time-based on a mitonuclear communication mechanism that controls the tRNA ligase HSPC117 in human cells.

works.title: Immune surveillance of cellular damage: lessons from Caenorhabditis elegans
works.abstract: Innate immune systems must detect infection rapidly and reliably, yet pathogens can often evade direct recognition by host pattern-recognition receptors. An alternative and increasingly appreciated strategy is damage-driven immune surveillance, whereby hosts detect pathogen-induced perturbations to essential cellular and tissue functions rather than microbial molecules themselves. This mode of detection is particularly prominent in Caenorhabditis elegans, which lacks professional immune cells and most canonical innate immune receptors, and therefore relies extensively on monitoring disruptions to core homeostatic pathways. Perturbations to protein translation, proteostasis, mitochondrial function, genome and nucleolar integrity, lysosomal homeostasis, and Golgi function can all trigger immune responses. Recent studies have further uncovered roles for inter-organelle communication, effector-triggered surveillance of lysosome-related organelles, and physiological signals such as intestinal distension in regulating immune activation. Here, we integrate these advances into an organelle- and tissue-centric framework and explore parallels with other organisms to identify emerging and potentially conserved principles of damage sensing in innate immunity. These findings highlight the surveillance of cellular homeostasis as a central strategy for immunity that operates beyond canonical pattern-recognition mechanisms.

works.title: Distinct core minor pilin complexes prime specialized type IV filaments in cyanobacteria
works.abstract: The model cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 encodes, in addition to the major pilin of the Type IV pilus filament, an extensive, partially uncharacterized repertoire of minor pilins. For those cyanobacterial minor pilins that have been characterized, their roles span a surprisingly diverse range of functions. To elucidate the roles of uncharacterized minor pilins in a systematic way, we applied structural phylogenomics across 90 genomes, classifying cyanobacterial pilins into six conserved families that form two distinct putative core priming complexes. We demonstrate that these complexes initiate the assembly of two morphologically distinct Type IV pilus filaments: short, hyper-dynamic pili for natural competence, and long, adhesive pili for motility and phototaxis. Structural analysis revealed a conserved β-solenoid domain in PilX subunits, which we propose fulfills the capping function of PilY1 homologs. Proteomic data indicate that the minor pilin PilX2 facilitates the assembly of motility pili, which is required to maintain DnaJ3 co-chaperone levels and trigger cAMP-dependent surface sensing. These findings challenge the concept of a single multipurpose pilus, establishing that cyanobacteria utilize a shared machinery to assemble two specialized filaments, each primed by distinct core minor pilin complexes to meet the conflicting biophysical requirements of DNA uptake and surface motility.

works.title: Extensive mobilome heterogeneity in a widespread endosymbiont: A candidate dimeric plasmid and highly fragmented prophages in Wolbachia from Culex pipiens
works.abstract: The obligate, intracellular bacteria Wolbachia have gained increasing interest due to their selfish modifications of host arthropod reproduction, impacts on host evolution, and utility in vector control efforts to reduce arbovirus transmission worldwide. Despite their highly reduced genomes, Wolbachia harbor a rich mobilome that includes phages, insertion sequences and plasmids in mosquito vectors. However, these repeat-rich mobile genetic elements are notoriously difficult to assemble and can generate artificial, chimeric sequences that obscure their true diversity. As a result, conventional genome sequencing and assembly approaches often fail to resolve the complexity, leaving critical gaps of knowledge on how these elements evolve, mobilize, and shape both symbiont and host genomes. To address these challenges, we established a novel Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing strategy that avoids prior PCR amplification and leverages single-dissected, female ovaries. Using this approach, we report and characterize-directly from native long-read molecules-the first near-complete Wolbachia genome and its mobile elements from individual ovaries of the mosquito vector Culex pipiens molestus. Additional short reads from individuals of the same strain were used to assess and validate candidate mutations, particularly in repetitive regions. We report a new dimeric structure of the pWCP plasmid, suggesting the existence of multimeric plasmid forms potentially associated with active replication. We also observed extensive fragmentation of prophage WO regions despite long read sequencing, underscoring their structural complexity. Raw long read analyses recovered multiple alternative gene syntenies within WO regions, pointing to heterogeneous prophage architectures missed by the assembly and marked diversity of WO elements in Wolbachia of Culex pipiens (wPip) group strains. Taken together, our results illuminate the structural heterogeneity of the endosymbiont genome that is shaped by integrated and episomal mobile elements.

works.title: Auxilin in enteroendocrine cells controls intestinal homeostasis through inter-cell signaling relays
works.abstract: Adult stem cells are critical for the homeostasis of residential tissue and organism fitness. Residential stem cells must constantly perceive external and internal signals and adjust their proliferation rate accordingly to avoid unlimited proliferation or premature differentiation. However, how differentiated cells affect stem cell proliferation and tissue homeostasis through cell-cell communication still remains poorly understood. Here, we unveil an unprecedented function of Auxilin (Aux) in enteroendocrine cells (EEs) by restricting intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation. aux depletion in all EEs leads to intestinal homeostasis disruption. The levels of Slit are dramatically reduced in aux-depleted EEs and cytokine Upd3 expression is significantly increased in some aux-depleted EEs and neighboring wild type enterocytes (ECs). Ectopic expression of slit could effectively rescue the defects observed in prosts > auxRNAi intestines. Interestingly, EGFR signaling is ectopically activated due to EGFR accumulation in aux-depleted EEs. Further inhibiting EGFR signaling completely suppresses the defects in prosts > auxRNAi intestines. Finally, EGFR signaling suppresses slit transcription by Pointed binding to slit regulatory regions. Together, these data show that Aux in EEs restrains ISCs from excessive proliferation and aberrant progeny differentiation to maintain intestinal homeostasis through inter-cell communications. Thus our study uncovers the underlying mechanism of how stem cell proliferation is properly controlled by differentiated cells through inter-cell signaling relays during tissue homeostasis and tumorigenesis.

works.title: Phylogenomics of Cypriniformes, the most diverse order of freshwater fishes: consensus, challenges, and limitations
works.abstract: Cypriniformes, the most species-rich order of freshwater fishes (∼5,000 species), represents a key lineage for understanding vertebrate diversification in freshwater ecosystems. This clade includes several highly miniaturized and understudied lineages whose phylogenetic placements have long remained contentious. Here, we present the first phylogenomic analysis of Cypriniformes with complete family-level representation and broad genus-level coverage, encompassing 316 species comprising ∼30% of all described genera. Our dataset integrates 257 newly assembled genomes with publicly available resources and analyzes multiple sets of genome-wide markers using both concatenation-based and coalescent-aware approaches. The general concordance among analytical frameworks indicates that the backbone topology of Cypriniformes is now established, allowing clear identification of well-supported clades and regions of persistent conflict. Our results strengthen the evolutionary relationships of several miniaturized lineages, while identifying recalcitrant relationships shaped by both biological processes and model artifacts that can yield superficially similar patterns of phylogenetic conflict. Our study substantially expands genomic representation and establishes a phylogenomic foundation for future comparative, developmental, and evolutionary research in this freshwater radiation.

works.title: scEvoSel maps evolutionary selection signals onto single-cell transcriptomic atlases to reveal selection-relevant cellular contexts
works.abstract: Selection is a core driving force of evolution. Although genome-wide scanning can identify numerous genomic regions affected by selection, it remains challenging to further reveal the specific cellular contexts in which these selection signals act. To address this issue, we developed scEvoSel, an analytical framework that integrates population-level selection signals with single-cell RNA sequencing data to identify selection-relevant cell types. We calculated DCMS scores based on the population variation data from wild boars and domestic pigs and mapped them to the single-cell atlas of skeletal muscle from wild boars and Duroc pigs. The results showed that scEvoSel accurately identified fibro-adipogenic progenitors (FAPs) and myocytes, which exhibited significant changes in cell proportions, as well as lymphoid cells, which showed breed-associated transcriptional divergence. Moreover, we also calculated DCMS scores derived from population variation data of red junglefowl and Leghorn chickens and mapped them to the single-cell atlas of the liver of Leghorn chicken. Hepatocytes, endothelial cells, Kupffer cells and B cells were identified by scEvoSel as the primary selection-relevant cell types. Additionally, scEvoSel enables the analysis of key genes and functional pathways affected by selection within the corresponding cellular contexts. Overall, scEvoSel provides a framework for resolving population selection signals at single-cell resolution, expands the research dimensions for functional interpretation of selection signals, and offers a methodological tool for investigating cellular contexts associated with selection-driven evolutionary processes and complex trait formation.

works.title: Genome shock in a migratory songbird hybrid zone
works.abstract: The genome shock hypothesis proposes that hybridization destabilizes genome regulation, leading to increased chromatin accessibility, derepression of transposable elements (TEs), and potential reductions in hybrid fitness, contributing to speciation. While extensively studied in plants, evidence in vertebrates is limited. Here, we tested this hypothesis in a hybrid zone between two subspecies of Swainson's thrushes (Catharus ustulatus). We quantified genome-wide TE proportions, TE expression, and chromatin accessibility during both the migratory and non-migratory state using whole genome resequencing, RNA-seq, and ATAC-seq data from two migration-associated brain regions. Hybrids exhibited greater TE proportions, expression, and chromatin accessibility than parental lineages, providing the first direct evidence for genome shock in a wild avian system. TE expression and chromatin accessibility were positively correlated in all states and brain regions, but the strength of these patterns differed between states and tissues indicating that genome shock is context-dependent. Signatures of shock were localized in regulatory regions and associated with differential transcript factor binding sites linked to retinoic acid receptor signaling, a key pathway for seasonal and photoperiodic responses. Overlap between open chromatin, upregulated TEs and previously identified transgressively expressed genes in these hybrids suggest that genome shock extends beyond TE activation to directly affect gene expression. Our results motivate further investigation into genome shocks' effects on genomic incompatibilities, hybrid fitness, and speciation.

works.title: FlyBase: Development and metamorphosis into the Alliance
works.abstract: FlyBase (flybase.org) is an openly accessible, centralized resource for genetic, genomic and functional data about Drosophila melanogaster. This article describes recent updates to the curation and display of expression, functional and reagent data within FlyBase, including the incorporation of long-read RNA-seq data, the introduction of the 'Gene ToolKit' for identifying key genetic reagents, and new reports for protein complexes, metabolic pathways and combinations of split-GAL4 drivers. We also provide information on changes to our data archiving policy and guidance on how best to use AI methods to interrogate FlyBase. Finally, we give an update on the status of transitioning FlyBase into the Alliance of Genome Resources.

works.title: Locating Lewontin on the genotype–phenotype map
works.abstract: Over the last century, evolutionary genetics has steadily advanced our understanding of the architecture of simple and complex traits of individuals among diverse organisms. In this context, Tautz et al. (2026), in their Perspective “Beyond Mendel: a call to revisit the genotype–phenotype map through new experimental paradigms,” call for genetics to move beyond one-gene-one-trait thinking toward developing experimental approaches to embrace pleiotropy, epistasis, and context-dependent complexity in the genotype–phenotype (G–P) map. They emphasize the limits of what they believe are conventional approaches to genetic analyses, including missing heritability. We were struck by the absence of any mention of Lewontin's (1974a) G–P map concept in Tautz et al.'s Perspective. Lewontin's scheme represents interconnections among multilocus genotype, development, and phenotype. This omission may be accidental, but it points to a persistent divide among population, quantitative, and molecular genetics. That gap motivates our aim in this letter: to show how three of Lewontin's ideas complement those of Tautz et al.: units of selection, norms of reaction, multilocus interactions and genome complexity.

works.title: Brr2p-mediated unwinding of U4/U6 is promoted by a mutually exclusive internal stem loop in U4 and involves destabilization of the 5’ stem-loop of U4
works.abstract: Before the spliceosome engages a pre-mRNA to excise its introns, the catalytic small nuclear RNA (snRNA) U6 is inactive because of base pairing with U4 snRNA; thus, spliceosome activation requires unwinding of base paired U4/U6, composed of stem I and stem II. The Ski2-like ATPase and RNA helicase Brr2p facilitates U4/U6 unwinding and the ultimately irreversible release of U4; however, the molecular mechanism behind Brr2p-mediated U4/U6 unwinding and the roles of the snRNAs in unwinding remain incompletely understood. To investigate the mechanism in vivo in budding yeast, we screened an unwinding-deficient, cold-sensitive brr2 mutant, associated with retinitis pigmentosa in humans, for genetic interactions with mutations in U4 snRNA. Some destabilizing U4 mutations in either stem I or stem II suppressed the brr2 mutant, providing functional evidence that Brr2p disrupts both stems in vivo. Further, destabilizing mutations in the intervening 5’ stem loop of U4 also suppressed the brr2 mutant, and in vitro Brr2p displaced Prp31p from this stem loop, implicating Brr2p in disruption of this structure, too. Unexpectedly and counterintuitively, a subset of destabilizing mutations in U4/U6 stem I exacerbated the brr2 mutant. These mutations disrupted a conserved, internal stem loop in U4 that is mutually exclusive with U4/U6 stem I. In yeast, we found that this stem loop (U4-ISL1) is required for splicing in vivo and for U4/U6 unwinding in vitro. Notably, this stem loop overlaps with a region of human RNU4-2 mutated in neurodevelopmental disorders.
