Imputation of fluid intelligence to increase power for gene discovery
The landscape of gene loss and missense variation across the mammalian tree informs on gene essentiality
works.abstract: Abstract Patterns of gene and sequence preservation across species provide insight into gene essentiality under natural selection. Here we developed two interspecies constraint metrics across 462 mammalian species: Gene Identity Score of Mammalian Orthologs (GISMO), which quantifies gene loss weighted by evolutionary distance to humans, and GISMO-mis, which measures missense constraint using the ratio of missense to synonymous variation across mammals. Both metrics are strongly correlated with human loss of function, missense and dosage constraint derived from large-scale sequencing studies, yet are largely independent of coding sequence length. GISMO and GISMO-mis identify essential genes missed by existing human-only metrics, particularly short genes. Genes in the most constrained deciles are enriched for rare variant associations in disorders linked to reduced fecundity, including schizophrenia, autism and neurodevelopmental disorders, and show strong enrichment for common variant heritability. These deciles also exhibit reduced copy number variation, consistent with dosage sensitivity. In addition, GISMO improves prioritization of recessive disease genes and captures signatures of homozygous selection across the mammalian tree. Taken together, GISMO and GISMO-mis leverage deep mammalian evolution to provide complementary, length-robust measures of gene essentiality that strengthen disease–gene prioritization and illuminate the selective forces shaping human biology.

works.title: Small variant calling in the era of long-read sequencing
Proteome-wide C-degron activity profiling connects conditional regulation of the CTLH E3 ligase complex to ribosome biogenesis
works.abstract: Many E3 ubiquitin ligases recognize degrons located at protein termini, but the paucity of bona fide substrates of N-degron and C-degron pathways hampers our understanding of their physiological significance. Devising an expression screening strategy to assess the effect of C-terminal “capping” on the stability of thousands of human proteins, we systematically identify substrates harboring C-degrons. Interrogating one leading candidate, ZMYND19, we characterize a C-degron pathway governed via the C-terminal to LisH (CTLH) E3 ligase complex subunit Muskelin. Cell-to-cell variability in ZMYND19 stability uncovered conditional regulation, with CTLH-mediated degradation impaired by TNF-α stimulation but enhanced by mTOR inhibition. Parallel genetic and proteomic screens identified angio-associated migratory protein (AAMP) and apoptosis-enhancing nuclease (AEN) as additional substrates of the CTLH Muskelin C-degron pathway, leading us to define an essential role for AAMP in ribosome maturation through chaperone activity toward uL16. Altogether, these data define a C-degron pathway connecting conditional regulation of the CTLH E3 ligase complex to ribosome biogenesis.

works.title: Regulatable in vivo gene expression via adaptamers
MineGraph facilitates plastid and mitochondrial graph pangenome analysis in plants
works.abstract: The rapid growth of genomic sequencing is driving the implementation of graph pangenomes in evolutionary studies, yet the computational costs and complex interpretations at higher taxonomic levels hinder their broad use. Here, we present an evolutionary graph pangenome (evograph) pipeline to streamline diversity analyses across species and families. Applying this framework to 709 Poales chloroplast genomes indicates that genomic diversity is driven primarily by species-specific variation. We resolve a 77.7 Kbp consensus genome and apply graph theory metrics to highlight distinct genus-level evolutionary signatures. Evographs provide a powerful, nuanced framework for resolving evolutionary complexity across high taxonomic levels.

works.title: A novel CCMS model reveals a critical intronic sequence in the Snrpb gene that is required for normal development
works.abstract: Pathogenic variants in SNRPB, a common core spliceosomal factor, cause Cerebrocostomandibular Syndrome (CCMS). Most CCMS-associated variants result in increased inclusion of a PTC-containing alternative exon 2 (AE2). Using CRISPR/Cas9 we generated two mutant mice that carried a 46bp or a 61bp deletion upstream of Snrpb AE2. Mice and embryos carrying the 46bp deletion are normal. Whereas heterozygous and homozygous mutant embryos carrying the 61bp deletion (Δ61) exhibited smaller heads, micrognathia, malformations in the bones of the craniofacial region and ribs, and reduced survival, at low penetrance. Embryos homozygous for Δ61 showed a tendency towards increased inclusion of AE2 and reduced levels of Snrpb. In addition, this deletion increased the penetrance and severity of defects in Snrpbncc and Snrpbmes mutant embryos. Our findings indicate that this intronic region is important for SNRPB regulation in mice and should be investigated in CCMS patients that do not carry mutations in SNRPB coding exons.

works.title: Genomic in vitro transcription and Nanopore direct RNA sequencing of a human B-Lymphocyte cell line
works.abstract: Genomic DNA used as a template for in vitro transcription of RNA can serve as a true negative control for benchmarking RNA modification detection by Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) models. We generated DRS data for in vitro transcribed (IVT) RNA composed of canonical nucleotides using genomic DNA from a human cell line. We applied Dorado modification calling models to these data, and calculated 9-mer specific false-positive rates for eight RNA modifications as a comparison point for future development of RNA modification models.

works.title: Establishing Polycomb regulatory landscapes in human early development
RNA ends connect genetic risk to brain disease
Towards equitable population epigenomics: implications for global health
Golgi-associated tethers capture vesicles from specific membrane recycling pathways
works.abstract: During maturation of a Golgi cisterna, a series of vesicular transport pathways recycle resident Golgi proteins. Recycling vesicles are captured by Golgi-associated tethers. Here, we examined three of these recycling pathways in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. For each pathway, we determined which tethers were present on a maturing cisterna while the vesicles were arriving, and we ectopically localized different tethers to determine which ones captured the vesicles. Those approaches yielded mutually consistent results. At an intermediate stage of cisternal maturation, the golgin Sgm1 tethers vesicles from an intra-Golgi recycling pathway dependent on COPI. At a late stage of cisternal maturation, the golgin Imh1 and the multi-subunit GARP complex tether vesicles from an intra-Golgi recycling pathway dependent on the AP-1 and Ent5 clathrin adaptors. This involvement of GARP in intra-Golgi recycling had not previously been appreciated. We found no evidence for the earlier proposal that GARP tethers vesicles traveling from prevacuolar endosome compartments to the trans-Golgi network, but Imh1 does tether those vesicles. Our data contribute to an integrated and increasingly mechanistic picture of Golgi dynamics.

works.title: A USP28-TM9SF3-Golgiphagy axis maintains glycosylation homeostasis and promotes breast cancer progression
works.abstract: Selective autophagy of the Golgi apparatus (Golgiphagy) is essential for Golgi quality control, yet its regulation and physiological functions remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the deubiquitinase USP28 as an upstream regulator of the Golgiphagy receptor TM9SF3. USP28 removes degradative K48-linked ubiquitin chains from TM9SF3, preventing its proteasomal degradation and sustaining Golgiphagy under nutrient and Golgi stresses. CRM1-dependent nuclear export enables the stress-induced translocation of USP28 to the Golgi, where it stabilizes TM9SF3, promoting Golgi fragmentation and autophagic clearance. Loss of USP28 or TM9SF3 impairs Golgiphagy, disrupts glycosylation fidelity, and inhibits breast cancer cell proliferation. Proteomic and functional analyses identify the glycosyltransferase MGAT5 as a selective TM9SF3-dependent Golgiphagy cargo, revealing how this pathway maintains glycosylation homeostasis. In syngeneic tumor models, USP28 knockout or pharmacological inhibition reduces TM9SF3 abundance, compromises Golgiphagy, perturbs glycosylation, and markedly suppresses tumor growth-effects restored by wild-type but not LC3-binding-deficient TM9SF3. Together, these findings reveal a USP28-TM9SF3-Golgiphagy axis that couples ubiquitin signaling to Golgi glycosylation control and represents a therapeutically targetable pathway for breast cancer.

works.title: ATP-driven dynamics and itraconazole binding of the drug efflux pump Cdr1 from Candida glabrata
works.abstract: Azole resistance in Candida species is often caused by the overexpression of Cdr1. Despite its clinical relevance, the structural basis for its ATP-driven efflux pump function remains elusive. We present four high-resolution cryo-EM structures of Candida glabrata Cdr1 obtained in the absence and presence of ATP-Mg²⁺, itraconazole, and vanadate, capturing distinct nucleotide- and substrate-occupancy states. Additional low-population cryo-EM conformers were unveiled by 3D variability analysis, offering a detailed view of structural transitions linked with ATP-hydrolysis. The motion shows a 4 Å piston-like retraction of the C-helix from the γ-phosphate/vanadate of the hydrolyzed ATP. This causes the nearby transmembrane helix-1 (TMH-1) to open the drug-binding site via lateral displacement and unwinding of the inner-leaflet region of TMH-2. A reverse 'squeeze-and-push' motion of TMH-2 possibly drives substrate extrusion. High-resolution structures also reveal how itraconazole adapts its shape to fit into the drug-binding site. Our findings provide a dynamic structural framework for Cdr1-mediated azole resistance and the conserved chemo-mechanical cycle of ABC proteins, including non-membranous members.

works.title: Early holobiont-level divergence and adaptation across seafloor geochemical contrasts in the deep-sea squat lobster Shinkaia crosnieri
works.abstract: Deep-sea hydrothermal vents and methane seeps host unique animal communities sustained by chemosynthetic symbioses, yet how biological diversification proceeds across these geochemically distinct and geographically fragmented habitats remains poorly understood. Previous studies have largely focused on either host genomic adaptation or symbiont diversity as drivers of isolation, leaving unresolved how environmental geochemistry and host-microbe associations jointly shape evolutionary trajectories in chemosynthetic ecosystems. Here, we addressed this gap by combining chromosome-level host genomics, population resequencing, and episymbiont metagenomics in the deep-sea chemosynthetic lobster Shinkaia crosnieri, a dominant species inhabiting both hydrothermal vents and methane seeps. Genomic innovations-including sensory tradeoffs (vision loss versus chemosensory expansion), metabolic compensation for pigment loss, and positive selection on respiratory protein-underpin deep-sea colonization of S. crosnieri. Populations from the Okinawa Trough vent and the South China Sea seep exhibit pronounced genetic divergence, potentially driven by Pleistocene vicariance and reinforced by divergent selection across sulfur-enriched (vent) versus sulfur-depleted, methane-dominated (seep) environments. This selection targets host genes involved in chemoreception and immunity, with coordinated signatures in both sequence evolution and structural variation. Crucially, holobiont-level adaptation is amplified by habitat-specific recruitment of episymbionts: sulfur-oxidizing Campylobacterales/Thiotrichales dominate vent-associated lobsters, while methanotrophic Methylococcales prevail at seep counterparts. These symbionts partition energy niches metabolically, with seep-associated communities enhancing biosynthesis of key cofactors (e.g. coenzyme Q, tetrahydrofolate). Host transporters for these nutrients are concurrently upregulated, demonstrating functional synergy. Our findings establish that diversification in extreme environments operates holobiont-wide, where geochemical gradients synergistically shape host genomic plasticity and symbiont metabolic specialization to drive early-stage divergence.

works.title: Introgression under linear selection on continuous genomes
works.abstract: We model the introgression of a small block that carries many weakly selected linked loci into a large homogeneous population, under the simple assumption that a block of introduced genome has a selective effect proportional to its map length. Using a diffusion approximation, we compute the probability that some part of the initial block survives the initial phase of the introgression and give the typical length of the surviving blocks. Our results quantify the effect of recombination on selection and drift during an introgression and indicate that the fate of the block depends on the strength of selection relative to recombination. When selection is positive some parts of the block are able to survive at large times, but large blocks can only persist if selection is stronger than recombination. Surprisingly, the probability of such a successful introgression is independent of the strength of recombination and is the same as that for a single beneficial allele. (This is not true of other quantities.) Conversely, a deleterious or neutral block is eventually lost, but at a much slower rate than a single allele with the same selective effect. In this case, surviving blocks are very small. We also consider the introgression of a block of genome made of a single beneficial allele linked to a deleterious background and compute the amount of deleterious material that hitchhikes during fixation.

works.title: A History of FlyBase Prelude, Remembrance & Requiem
Multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM): a reconfigurable platform for high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy
works.abstract: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) enables gentle, rapid and efficient volumetric imaging of biological specimens. Despite its potential, LSFM has fragmented into multiple variants, each narrowly optimized for specific samples or imaging regimes, limiting its broad applicability. Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains diffraction-limited performance across a refractive index range of 1.33 to 1.51. It is compatible with standard sample mounting, current clearing protocols and high-throughput 3D imaging. We leverage miOPM to image diverse biological specimens at multiple spatial scales. By expanding the adaptability and ease of use of LSFM, miOPM is poised to democratize advanced 3D imaging. The multi-immersion oblique plane microscope is a flexible and versatile light-sheet microscope that allows imaging of samples ranging from cells in culture to whole organisms or cleared tissue samples.

works.title: APR-Score: Identification and Scoring of Aggregation-prone Regions in Protein Sequences
works.abstract: Protein aggregation is a critical phenomenon associated with numerous neurodegenerative and systemic diseases. Understanding the propensity of proteins to aggregate is essential for unraveling the molecular basis of these disorders and for the design and engineering of novel proteins, as well as for modulating the activity/stability of enzymatic proteins. Here, we present APR-Score, a novel machine learning-based computational method designed to identify aggregation-prone regions within protein sequences. APR-Score leverages a combination of sequence-based features to predict regions of proteins that are prone to aggregation. It harnessed the information embedded in compiled sequence and structural features to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy. The method was evaluated through rigorous cross-validation on the training dataset and further validated on an independent test dataset. APR-Score demonstrated robustness and reliability in distinguishing aggregation-prone regions from non-aggregating ones, achieving a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.77, precision of 0.89, and F1-Score of 0.87. This tool offers significant value for researchers investigating protein aggregation-related diseases, as it can expedite the identification of aggregation-prone regions, thereby aiding the development of targeted therapies and diagnostic tools. Moreover, computational protein design and engineering efforts can be facilitated by APR-Score-based identification and screening of aggregation-prone protein sequences. APR-Score is available at https://github.com/TII-BRC/APR-Score.

works.title: Combining MAVEs and computational predictors improves variant classification across ancestries in hereditary cancer genes
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Many commonly used computational tools for variant effect prediction exhibit ancestry-related bias because they are trained on clinical or population datasets that under-represent global diversity, leading to uneven and sometimes unfair variant classification across ancestries. Multiplexed assays of variant effect (MAVEs) and population-free variant effect predictors (VEPs) instead offer alternatives that are unbiased with respect to human ancestry, providing classification evidence that generalises across populations. METHODS: Here, we evaluate MAVE- and VEP-based classification across five cancer-associated genes with high-quality MAVE datasets, focusing primarily on three leading population-free VEPs: GEMME, EVE, and CPT-1. RESULTS: We find that MAVEs are more conservative and decisive in classification, assigning fewer variants to the pathogenic category while yielding fewer indeterminate classifications when calibrated to ACMG/AMP guidelines. Although MAVEs show heightened sensitivity in functionally assayed regions, VEPs identify a broader range of pathogenic variants overall. By combining clinical evidence strengths from MAVEs and VEPs, we reclassify over 90% of variants of uncertain significance across the SG10K_Health and Mexico City Prospective Study reference datasets as at least likely benign or likely pathogenic. We further isolate variants where MAVE- and VEP-based classifications are discordant, highlighting method-specific limitations. CONCLUSIONS: Together, these findings clarify the complementary strengths of experimental and computational classification approaches and provide a path to less biased and more equitable variant interpretation in clinical genomics, helping to mitigate disparities in diagnosis across ancestries.

works.title: Amira: detection of single and multi-copy antimicrobial resistance genes directly from long reads using gene-space de Bruijn graphs
works.abstract: Abstract Accurate detection of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes is essential for AMR surveillance and genotypic prediction. Current approaches typically either depend on a correct genome assembly or use k-mers directly from the reads. However AMR genes are often multicopy and are enriched at repeat loci where genome assemblers tend to fail, and k-mer methods struggle to distinguish different copies. We present Amira, which detects AMR genes directly from long reads by building gene-space de Bruijn graphs, allowing precise association of reads with distinct AMR gene copies, enabling accurate assembly. Across simulations, curated samples, and public datasets, Amira improves copy-number recall and nucleotide accuracy compared with existing methods.

works.title: Microtubule pushing and cortical pulling cooperate to orient and position the mitotic spindle
works.abstract: While regulation of spindle positioning and orientation is known to be mediated by cortical pulling forces generated by dynein on astral microtubules, the contribution of microtubule-based pushing forces remains less clear. We developed a two-dimensional computational model that incorporates both cortical pulling and microtubule pushing to examine spindle behavior across diverse cell types and geometries. The model successfully recapitulates experimental observations in cells that round during mitosis, including Drosophila follicular epithelial cells, Drosophila neuroblasts, and the early C. elegans embryo. Our analysis shows that pulling forces are the dominant determinants of directional spindle orientation. However, pushing forces play essential supporting roles by preventing spindle stalling, enhancing robustness, and facilitating efficient alignment. We further applied our model to irregularly shaped zebrafish endothelial cells, which exhibit complex, non-spherical geometries and dynamic morphology. In this context, our model demonstrates that asymmetric distributions of cortical force generators, potentially enriched at cell-cell junctions, are sufficient to explain off-center spindle positioning. Together, this work establishes a unified framework linking cell geometry, molecular polarity cues, and force balance to spindle dynamics.

works.title: Charting brain structure in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome with clinical neuroimaging
authors: the ENIGMA 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome Working Group
Marianne B. M. van den Bree
works.abstract: Abstract Background 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) is a common microdeletion associated with widespread brain alterations and elevated risk for schizophrenia and other neuropsychiatric conditions. Prospective research studies often exclude individuals with severe cognitive impairment, medical comorbidities, or inability to tolerate research magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without sedation, features common in 22q11DS and other rare genetic disorders. This limits both the generalizability of neuroimaging findings and our understanding of the full phenotypic spectrum. Moreover, while standard brain growth charts quantify deviation from typical development, they cannot identify patients who are disproportionately affected relative to their genetic peers, limiting clinical utility for risk stratification. Leveraging clinical MRI data offers a scalable approach to address these gaps. Methods In this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we analyzed 92 patients with 22q11DS (age 0.5–21 years, 49% female) and 252 matched clinical controls. Using normative modeling derived from 1,995 reference clinical scans, we quantified patient brain deviations from population norms. We validated clinical findings against the independent ENIGMA-22q research consortium, characterized rates of extreme structural deviations to assess within-syndrome heterogeneity, correlated spatial patterns of brain alterations with gene expression from the Allen Human Brain Atlas, and generated syndrome-specific growth charts to test whether deviations from syndrome-specific norms predicted cognitive and language outcomes. Results Patients with 22q11DS showed widespread reductions in brain volumes (max Cohen’s d = −1.31) and cortical surface area (d = −0.71) with increased cortical thickness (d = 0.39). These findings were highly convergent with the ENIGMA-22q research cohort ( r = 0.61–0.87). Forty percent of patients showed at least one global brain measure below the 2.5th centile. Spatial patterns of cortical volume and surface area correlated with expression of genes within the 22q11.2 locus. In exploratory analyses, syndrome-specific growth chart deviations in cerebellar volumes relative to 22q11DS peers were nominally associated with lower language scores across two independent assessment methods ( p < 0.03), suggesting potential prognostic utility. Conclusions This study provides a critical proof of principle for using heterogeneous clinical imaging to robustly characterize brain structure in rare genetic disorders. Syndrome-specific growth charts provide a novel framework to quantify within-syndrome variability and demonstrate potential prognostic value by linking individual brain structure to cognitive outcomes.

works.title: Longitudinal single-cell and spatial profiling of sonic hedgehog medulloblastoma identifies novel therapeutic targets
works.abstract: Abstract Background Sonic hedgehog (SHH) medulloblastoma (MB) accounts for approximately one-third of all MB cases, the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Despite therapy, SHH MB relapse is frequent and has a dismal prognosis. New treatments for recurrent SHH MB are needed; however, the molecular drivers of relapse are poorly understood. Methods We profiled 22 SHH MB specimens (16 primary and 6 recurrent), including four primary–recurrent patient pairs, using overlapping single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq; n = 16), single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (snATAC-seq; n = 13), and spatial transcriptomic ( n = 6) cohorts. We integrated these data with exome-derived variant calls from 25 specimens, including seven patients with primary and recurrent samples. Bulk RNA-seq data from 48 specimens representing 24 primary–recurrent pairs were used for validation. Results Our analyses show evidence of positive selection for nonsynonymous tumor mutations, including TP53 mutations involving its DNA-binding and tetramerization domains. TP53 mutations were associated with reduced base-excision repair (BER) gene expression and accessibility of linked cis-regulatory regions. Recurrent tumors showed increased tumor mutational burden (TMB) and an endoplasmic-reticulum (ER) stress expression program associated with poorer survival. Angiogenic gene expression and inferred immunosuppressive myeloid signaling were increased in recurrent disease. Conclusions These data define recurrence-associated cellular and regulatory programs, nominate candidate therapeutic targets and prognostic markers, and provide a single-cell and spatial atlas of SHH MB.

works.title: Development and validation of a trans‑ancestry polygenic risk score for coronary artery disease in the chinese population
works.abstract: Trans-ancestry polygenic risk scores (PRSs) have been proposed to address the limited transferability of European-specific PRSs to East Asian populations. However, their ability to improve risk prediction for coronary artery disease (CAD) in the Chinese population remains unclear. We aimed to develop and validate a trans-ancestry CAD PRS in the Chinese population by integrating European and East Asian genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Using summary statistics from large-scale CAD GWAS meta-analyses of East Asian and European populations, we constructed trans-ancestry PRSs via PRS-CSx in two configurations: PRS-meta, derived exclusively from GWAS results and linkage disequilibrium reference panels; and PRS-combine, optimized in a Chinese training set comprising 2,800 CAD cases and 2,055 controls. For comparison, we generated East Asian-specific PRSs using LDpred and pruning-and-thresholding methods, and additionally evaluated previously published CAD PRSs. The top-performing PRSs for each method in the training set were then externally validated in 72,782 individuals with genetic data from the China Kadoorie Biobank (CKB), a large-scale population-based cohort in China, with a mean follow-up of 12.1 years. In the training set, PRS-meta and PRS-combine exhibited comparable predictive performance, with odds ratios per standard deviation (SD) of 2.21 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.04, 2.38) and 2.23 (95% CI: 2.06, 2.41), respectively. Both trans-ancestry PRSs showed approximately 60% and 90% increases in pseudo-R 2 relative to the top-performing East Asian-specific and European-specific PRSs, respectively. In the CKB cohort, both scores were similarly associated with incident CAD, with hazard ratios (HRs) per SD of 1.33 (95% CI: 1.27, 1.41) for PRS-meta and 1.31 (95% CI: 1.24, 1.38) for PRS-combine. Individuals in the top versus bottom quintile had HRs of 2.06 (95% CI: 1.75, 2.42) for PRS-meta and 1.84 (95% CI: 1.56, 2.16) for PRS-combine. The trans-ancestry PRS constructed via PRS-CSx markedly improved CAD risk prediction in the Chinese population. This finding highlights an efficient and generalizable approach to developing more equitable PRSs for underrepresented populations, with PRS-meta demonstrating particular promise.

works.title: Multikingdom and functional gut microbiota markers for cholangiocarcinoma
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: While the association between gut microbiota and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) has been explored, existing research has been limited to bacterial components. The alterations in non-bacterial members (fungi, archaea, and viruses) and their functional characteristics in CCA remain unclear. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize the multi-kingdom gut microbiota and functional profiles in CCA patients and develop a non-invasive diagnostic model. METHODS: We performed metagenomic sequencing on 700 fecal samples collected from three distinct regions in China, comprising 289 CCA patients, 312 healthy controls, and 99 hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients. Multi-kingdom microbial composition and functional profiles were analyzed. We integrated multiple machine learning algorithms to generate 117 distinct modeling schemes for constructing and screening the optimal CCA diagnostic model. The model was validated across three independent cohorts and tested for specificity against HCC. We also benchmarked the model against established diagnostic approaches by reviewing 15 CCA clinical practice guidelines/consensus statements and their cited evidence and by evaluating model detection in CA19-9-positive and CA19-9-negative patients. RESULTS: Extensive alterations were identified in CCA patients across multi-kingdom and functional layers, including 198 archaeal, 154 bacterial, 78 fungal, and 120 viral species, as well as 278 genes, 99 pathways, and 151 carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes). A panel of 21 multi-kingdom and functional markers demonstrated superior diagnostic accuracy with an average AUC of 91% across three validation cohorts, outperforming any single-kingdom model. The model exhibited high specificity in distinguishing CCA from HCC, achieving an AUC of 99.74% with a false positive rate of 11.11%. Benchmarking supported a complementary role as a noninvasive screening aid, the model showed pooled sensitivity and specificity of 96.2%, and 78.5%, respectively, and detected 97.6% of CA19-9-negative CCA cases. CONCLUSIONS: This study represents the first comprehensive characterization of multi-kingdom gut microbiome and functional markers in cholangiocarcinoma. Gut multi-kingdom and functional microbial signatures represent a promising noninvasive tool that may aid the screening and early identification of cholangiocarcinoma in high-risk populations, complementing existing diagnostic approaches.

works.title: Publisher Correction: Gb3 encodes a unique kinase fusion protein conferring greenbug resistance in wheat
works.abstract: In the version of the article initially published, in the “Oxylipin genes” panel of Fig. 5e, there were two “4 days” labels in the “COM” section. The right label has now been corrected to “8 days” in the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

works.title: Towards a rational terminology for cell types
Conditional diffusion for single-cell Hi-C data imputation and enhancement with scHiC-Diff
works.abstract: Single-cell high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (scHi-C) enables the analysis of cell-to-cell variability in three-dimensional (3D) genome organization, but its utility is severely limited by pervasive technical dropouts, leading to extremely sparse contact maps. Accurately identifying dropout events and imputing the corresponding missing chromatin contacts remains a challenging problem, as technical dropouts are confounded with genuine absences of chromatin interactions. Existing imputation and enhancement methods often rely on smoothing strategies or restrictive parametric likelihood assumptions, which may obscure fine-scale chromatin structures and cell-specific features. Here, we present scHiC-Diff, a conditional diffusion-based framework for scHi-C data imputation and enhancement. scHiC-Diff employs a forward process that progressively perturbs contact maps and a reverse denoising process that reconstructs chromatin interactions from noisy observations. To better capture long-range dependencies in complex 3D genome structures, scHi-C contact matrices are treated as masked images and modeled using a Diffusion Transformer (DiT). Across two complementary simulated datasets and three real scHi-C datasets, scHiC-Diff improves the recovery of chromatin interaction patterns and enhances downstream analyses compared with existing methods. Application to a developmental scHi-C dataset further demonstrates improved reconstruction of chromatin organization and enhanced chromatin loop detection.

works.title: Glucocorticoid regulation of the human noncoding genome
works.abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) are widely used anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive agents known to induce substantial changes in gene expression, yet their effects on noncoding RNAs such as long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) or microRNAs (miRNAs) remain poorly characterized. Here, we present the first comprehensive and systematic analysis of GC regulation of the noncoding genome across nine human primary cell types from both hematopoietic and nonhematopoietic lineages. In vitro GC treatment was applied to each cell type, with transcriptomic profiling (total RNA-seq and small RNA-seq) at 2 and 6 h posttreatment. We identify more than 2000 GC-responsive noncoding transcripts, including 654 annotated lncRNAs, 1376 novel lncRNAs, and 39 miRNAs. The noncoding RNA response to GCs is highly cell type dependent: 80% of GC-responsive lncRNAs and 97% of miRNAs are unique to a single cell type. Hematopoietic cells exhibit a greater magnitude of lncRNA induction compared with nonhematopoietic cells. Notably, GC treatment uncovers dozens of facultative, stimulus-dependent lncRNAs. GC-responsive transcripts span diverse lncRNA classes, with enrichment of host lncRNAs. In contrast, only a limited number of miRNAs are GC responsive. GC regulation of transcript abundance for miRNAs and their host lncRNAs appears to be independent. Our results, which are accessible through an interactive web application, establish a framework for studying how noncoding transcription contributes to physiological and clinical heterogeneity in GC responses. The newly identified GC-responsive noncoding transcripts could represent biomarkers of GC exposure, determinants of GC sensitivity or resistance, or candidate regulators of tissue-specific GC effects.

works.title: Pangenome and transcriptomics reveal the genomic basis associated with interspecific variation of sexually dimorphic nuptial spines in moustache toads
works.abstract: Sexual dimorphism is a widespread phenotypic innovation that plays a crucial role in species diversification, yet its genetic origins and evolutionary trajectories remain poorly understood in vertebrates. Leptobrachium provides a tractable system in which male moustache toads develop maxillary nuptial spines used in male–male combat, whereas closely related pseudo-moustache toads lack this trait. To investigate the evolutionary genomics of these sexually dimorphic nuptial spines, we construct a pangenome from chromosome-level assemblies of six Leptobrachium species and integrate trans -species transcriptomic analyses. We find that keratin gene expansion predated the origin of nuptial spines, potentially providing genetic material for keratinized skin innovation. Recently duplicated hair keratin genes acquired putative Hoxc13 binding sites, and promoter reporter assays confirm that Hoxc13 can activate these genes in both moustache toads and pseudo-moustache toads. Differential hoxc13 expression may therefore be more important for affecting whether duplicated hair keratin genes are recruited to develop nuptial spines. Transcriptomic comparisons further reveal maxillary skin–specific expression of genes involved in keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, as well as melanogenesis during the formation of nuptial spines. In Leptobrachium tengchongense , which has undergone secondary loss of nuptial spines, igfbp2 , a conserved gene highly expressed in keratinized skin appendages across amphibians, shows positive selection and represents a candidate associated with this evolutionary transition. Our study provides amphibian pangenome resources and highlights how gene duplication coupled with regulatory recruitment may shape the evolution of novel sexually dimorphic traits in vertebrates.

works.title: Liver X receptors participate in the fasting response by assisting CEBPB binding to enhancers and promoting the fasting transcriptional program
works.abstract: Upon fasting, a group of transcription factors (TFs) activates an extensive transcriptional program in the liver to alter hepatocyte metabolism and cope with fasting. This is achieved by TF-mediated activation of enhancers, which become more accessible, leading to gene induction. Nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group H member 3 (NR1H3, also known as liver X receptor-alpha) and 2 (NR1H2, also known as liver X receptor-beta), collectively termed here LXRs, are important TFs known to participate in transcriptional programs in the fed state, but their role in fasting is unclear. Here, we examine the effect of LXR deletion on the transcriptional and chromatin programs activated in the fasted and fed states. We profile the liver transcriptome and genome-wide chromatin accessibility in single-knockout mice lacking either LXR isoform and in double-knockout mice lacking both isoforms. We find that double-knockout of LXRs impairs fasting-induced genes and enhancers. Analysis of genome-wide NR1H3 binding by ChIP-seq, together with chromatin accessibility profiling by ATAC-seq, shows that NR1H3 directly binds enhancers and increases their accessibility. We find that LXRs assist the binding of CCAAT enhancer binding protein beta (CEBPB) to enhancers during fasting. CEBPB is a key TF regulating the fasting response, and its genome-wide binding is perturbed in the absence of LXRs. Cooperation between LXRs and CEBPB promotes fasting-dependent gene induction. These findings reveal a previously unknown role for LXRs in the fasting response, whereby LXRs bind and increase enhancer accessibility, assist CEBPB binding, and promote gene induction. This study demonstrates the complex cooperation of TFs in regulating gene expression to maintain homeostasis during fasting and places LXRs as novel regulators of the fasting response.

works.title: GenoCLAMP: consolidation of sequence motifs from genomic-scale data
works.abstract: Genome-wide protein–DNA mapping studies have produced thousands of enriched sequence motifs, many of which are redundant because transcription factors (TFs) bind cooperatively as distinct complexes to shared sites. Here, we present Genomic CLustered Alignment of Motif Profiles (GenoCLAMP), an algorithm that unifies motif-clustering and alignment to collapse redundant motifs into high-quality merged matrix representations. We demonstrate that GenoCLAMP reliably recovers known TF complexes that bind common motifs and uncovers evidence for previously uncharacterized motifs. These results establish GenoCLAMP as a robust and efficient framework for motif consolidation, enhancing computational analyses and biological interpretation of large-scale TF–DNA binding datasets.

works.title: Electrostatic control of chromatin compaction safeguards against apoptotic DNA release
works.abstract: Apoptosis involves extensive intracellular reorganisation to facilitate the clearance of dying cells. A key step in this process is the destruction of the genome through fragmentation by caspase-activated DNase (CAD). Rather than dispersing after CAD-mediated cleavage, DNA fragments are compacted into a dense chromatin compartment, but the underlying mechanism and biological relevance of this compaction remain unknown. Here we show that global deacetylation of histone tails promotes chromatin compaction during apoptosis, preventing DNA release into apoptotic extracellular vesicles. Using synthetic effectors that modulate nucleosome electrostatics independently of histone modifications, we demonstrate that electrostatic attraction alone is sufficient to compact and sequester fragmented chromatin. These findings reveal a mechanism by which global reprogramming of histone modifications coordinates genome fragmentation with its physical sequestration during apoptosis. Our synthetic approach further provides a tool to probe how physical forces contribute to genome organisation across diverse biological contexts.

works.title: Revisiting the impact of synthetic ORF sequences on engineered LINE-1 retrotransposition
works.abstract: The retrotransposon Long Interspersed Element-1 (L1) contains adenosine rich open reading frames (ORFs), a characteristic that limits its expression in mammalian cells. A synthetic mouse L1 (smL1) with ORF adenosine content decreased from 40% to 26% showed increased mRNA expression and retrotransposed far more efficiently than the native parental element, L1spa (1). Here, we observe two nonsynonymous substitutions between the L1spa and smL1 ORF1 sequences and note that the smL1 3’UTR lacks a conserved guanosine-rich region (GRR) which could take on a G-quadruplex secondary structure. We find that the combined effect of the altered ORF1p amino acid sequence and the GRR 3’UTR deletion, rather than synthetic ORF sequences, accounts for the increase in smL1 retrotransposition efficiency over L1spa. We determine that inclusion of the GRR influences natural mouse L1 retrotransposition in a position-dependent manner that does not involve premature polyadenylation of L1 mRNA transcripts or alteration of L1 insertion structures. Instead, we present evidence that the position-dependent effect of the GRR on natural mouse retrotransposition occurs through modulation of L1 ORF1p abundance. In contrast, smL1 retrotransposition is refractory to the inhibitory effect of the GRR, likely owing to highly efficient protein expression from synthetic ORF sequences. Taken together, our results prompt further investigation of the relationship between the GRR sequence and L1 protein expression and demonstrate that the arrangement of L1 nucleotide sequences within reporter constructs can influence L1 expression and engineered retrotransposition efficiency.

works.title: NLGN3 autism variants have distinct functional impact on synapses and sleep behavior in Drosophila
works.abstract: Neuroligin-3 ( NLGN3 ) was first identified as a X-linked risk gene associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Most reported variants are identified in males who inherited their variants from an unaffected mother, but de novo variants have also been identified in both affected heterozygous females and hemizygous males. The p.R451C variant was the initial variant associating NLGN3 with ASD and has been heavily investigated, yet little is known about the functional consequences of other NLGN3 variants. To determine the functional consequences of other NLGN3 variants in vivo , we generated transgenic Drosophila models corresponding to a de novo variant (p.R175W) identified in a heterozygous female proband with ASD, a maternally inherited variant (p.R451C) identified in a hemizygous male with ASD, and another maternally inherited variant identified in a male (p.R597W) associated with sleep disorder and ASD. In Drosophila , loss of the fly homolog, Nlg3, altered sleep patterns, synaptic architecture, and vesicle dynamics, which were rescued by the expression of the human NLGN3 Ref allele. When comparing the variants, the p.R175W variant and the maternally inherited p.R451C variant altered synapse morphology with minimal effects on vesicle dynamics, and the p.R597W variant altered sleep and vesicle dynamics with minimal impact on synapse morphology. Using overexpression models, human NLGN3 Ref altered sleep patterns and synaptic morphology. Moreover, the p.R175W variant exacerbated sleep phenotypes, and the p.R175W and p.R451C variants exacerbated synapse morphology phenotypes. Together, our findings suggest that the de novo NLGN3 p.R175W variant identified in a heterozygous female exhibits gain-of-function properties, while maternally inherited variants have context-dependent functional impact. Moreover, some NLGN3 variants disrupt synaptic development, while other variants alter synaptic function, suggesting that NLGN3 variants have differential effects. These functional differences may provide insight into the heterogeneity of individuals with ASD.

works.title: Variant classification challenges in genes associated with multiple disorders contribute to the persistent interlaboratory discordance
works.abstract: Abstract Background Accurate germline variant classification requires correct application of ACMG/AMP evidence criteria and assignment of pathogenicity to a specific disease entity and mode of inheritance. Whether laboratories apply this disease-specific approach consistently to genes associated with multiple disorders remains insufficiently characterized. Methods We conducted a national interlaboratory study of germline variant classification using a proficiency-testing dataset comprising 13 variants across five clinical scenarios from 128 Chinese clinical genetic laboratories. Results Overall concordance was achieved for 6 of 13 variants, whereas 7 showed clinically meaningful cross-category discordance. Residual disagreement was partly attributable to omission or inappropriate use of ACMG/AMP evidence criteria, inconsistent strength assignment, and disease-context-specific interpretation. A prominent pattern of discordance involved disease-specific interpretation of variants in genes associated with multiple disorders. For variants in APOB , LZTR1 , MYH7 , and EPCAM , laboratories frequently transferred pathogenic assertions across disorders without adequately considering disease mechanism, inheritance pattern, or disorder-specific validity. By contrast, two GJB2 variants showed substantially higher categorical concordance. These errors could alter downstream clinical interpretation and, in some cases, implied management recommendations. Conclusions Disease-specific classification in multi-disease genes remains an important source of residual discordance despite improved criterion-level harmonization. Harmonization efforts should therefore extend beyond gene-level pathogenicity assessment toward mechanism-aware, disease-anchored classification frameworks and reporting practices. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

works.title: AmpliconSuite: an end-to-end workflow for analyzing focal amplifications in cancer genomes
works.abstract: Abstract Here we present AmpliconSuite, a toolkit for focal amplification analysis from cancer whole-genome sequencing that identifies extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), breakage–fusion–bridges and other amplification modes. Its ecContext module categorizes ecDNA structures to understand formation mechanisms. Validation across 175 metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization-probed genes in 72 models demonstrated accurate predictions. Analysis of 6,506 patient pan-cancer samples revealed ecDNA-mediated oncogene co-amplification preferences. To democratize data sharing, we created AmpliconRepository, a community-contributable platform, enabling investigation of results across >15,000 publicly hosted samples.

works.title: Recent developments of fluorescent proteins and biosensors driven by cross-disciplinary insights
Inherent electrochemical activity of extrachromosomal DNA hub shapes spatial redox environment in nucleus
The binding of OTULIN restrains LUBAC activity to prevent TNF-driven immunopathology
TraSPIN: inferring transporter specificity through language model-guided graph learning
works.abstract: Membrane transporters mediate cellular chemical exchange, yet their substrate specificities remain poorly characterized, with experimental studies constrained by the instability of membrane proteins. Existing computational tools often target narrow substrate classes or fail to generalize to distant homologs. We present TraSPIN, a geometric deep learning framework that jointly models transporter proteins and small-molecule substrates. TraSPIN outperforms existing methods, generalizes to unseen substrates and sequence-dissimilar transporters, and reveals structural determinants and sequence motifs of transporter–substrate recognition. Cross-species inference and de-orphanization of uncharacterized solute carrier proteins further demonstrate its utility for investigating transporter specificity and accelerating functional annotation.

works.title: Benchmarking long-read aligner-caller pipelines for structural variant detection across ten angiosperm species with PacBio high-fidelity sequencing
works.abstract: Structural variants (SVs) play a central role in genome evolution and phenotypic diversity, yet the large genome size, high repeat content, and structural complexity hinder SV detection in plants. Despite extensive benchmarking on human data, the performance and cross-species generalizability of HiFi long-read SV detection pipelines for plants have been overlooked. Here, we use multiple assembly-based variant calling strategies to construct SV truth sets at base-level resolution for ten representative angiosperm species, followed by systematic benchmarking of 91 HiFi-based SV calling pipelines. Cross-species evaluation reveals pronounced heterogeneity in performance across pipelines and species with deletion detection generally outperforming insertion detection. Using a stability score to quantify the across-species generalizability, we identify NGMLR/Sniffles2 and NGMLR/DeBreak as optimal cross-species pipelines for deletion detection, while Minimap2/Sniffles1, Minimap2/cuteSV2, and pbmm2/cuteSV1 exhibit robust insertion detection. We also find that detection accuracy declines sharply for large SVs and variants located within repetitive regions, particularly simple repeats. Moreover, SV calling precision shares a nonlinear relationship with sequencing depth for each individual haplotype, with F 1 scores peaking at ~ 15 × coverage. This study establishes a benchmarking framework for plant SV detection and provides high-confidence SV truth set resources that can, together, guide the selection of robust, scalable SV calling pipelines for plant genomics.

works.title: Commensal Lachnospiraceae bacterium mitigates colitis-induced mucin fucosylation deficits through ILC3/IL-22 axis
works.abstract: Flagellins from commensal bacteria are potent modulators of intestinal immunity, yet their strain-specific functions, particularly in promoting homeostasis in ulcerative colitis (UC), remain poorly defined. We investigate whether flagellin from the commensal Lachnospiraceae bacterium 3–1-57 FAA CT1 ( L. 3–1-57 Fla) plays a role in UC pathogenesis and mucin fucosylation deficits. Clinically, compared with healthy controls and patients with UC in remission, patients with active UC exhibit reduced abundance of L. 3–1-57 , which inversely correlates with disease severity. In mouse colitis models, we show that live L. 3–1-57 or L. 3–1-57 Fla attenuates intestinal inflammation and mucus barrier dysfunction, whereas E. coli flagellin exacerbates disease. Mechanistically, L. 3–1-57 Fla directly binds TLR5 with high affinity and activates dendritic cells to produce IL-23. This cascade expands IL-22 + group 3 innate lymphoid cells, drives fucosyltransferase 2-mediated MUC2 fucosylation, and restores mucus integrity. Crucially, genetic ablation of Tlr5 , inhibition of α-1,2-fucosylation, or IL-22 neutralization abolishes these benefits, confirming that the TLR5–IL-23–IL-22 immune axis and fucosylation are indispensable for protection. Our study establishes L. 3–1-57 flagellin as a key mediator of intestinal homeostasis via a TLR5–IL-23–IL-22-dependent mucin fucosylation pathway. These findings nominate L. 3–1-57 as a candidate next-generation probiotic, its flagellin as a potential postbiotic therapy for UC, and its fecal depletion as a potential noninvasive auxiliary diagnostic biomarker.

works.title: Extensive admixture and introgression shape genetic diversity and evolutionary adaptation in indigenous East Asian cattle
works.abstract: The complex introgression history of indigenous East Asian cattle is at the root of their remarkable diversity. Characterization of this diversity is a crucial step in understanding the genomic basis of adaptation to East Asian agricultural systems. However, the evolutionary history of indigenous East Asian cattle has remained poorly documented. Here, we present the largest short-read whole-genome sequencing dataset to date, including 802 indigenous Chinese cattle of 55 breeds/populations from diverse geographic regions, to address the population structure, genetic origins, and biological adaptations of this underrepresented population. We identify seven distinct genetic populations within Chinese cattle that were influenced by inter- and intraspecific introgression. We review introgression from Asian bovine species and reveal its geographical distribution characteristics in Chinese cattle. We identify a major taurine × indicine cattle admixture event during the Tang and Song dynasties (894–1210 AD ), which facilitated rapid local adaptation with a predominant effect on the immune system. Moreover, we present a comprehensive catalog of loci that underwent divergent selection across East Asian agroecological zones, including genes associated with cold tolerance, heat tolerance and meat production. Our findings indicate that admixture between taurine and indicine cattle, together with introgression from other Asian bovine species, contributed to the adaptive evolution of indigenous East Asian cattle.

works.title: Human DCM-time machine unravels cell state changes during primitive gut tube differentiation
works.abstract: Cell state changes in development and differentiation are directed by gene and enhancer activity dynamics, which are difficult to study in real time. We introduce the DCM-time machine into human induced pluripotent stem cells to enable retrospective, genome-wide tracing of transcriptional activity. This system labels active genes and enhancers with DCM methylation marks that are propagated during S-phase. Applied to differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells towards definitive endoderm and primitive gut tube, the DCM-time machine resolves activity dynamics and enables integration with transcription factor networks and CpG methylation profiles. Together, the human DCM-time machine provides a powerful platform for dissecting both healthy and pathogenic embryogenesis.

works.title: Dynamic landscapes of gene regulatory networks during early mammalian neurogenesis for understanding brain evolution and disorder risk
works.abstract: Neurogenesis is governed by dynamic transcriptional programs that vary across developmental time, brain region, and cell type, thereby forming regionally specialized neuronal circuits. However, the gene regulatory networks (GRNs) that coordinate these processes across species and brain regions are still not fully characterized. To address this, we construct a comprehensive GRN resource encompassing 24 neurogenic lineages from human, macaque, and mouse, enabling systematic cross-species and cross-regional comparisons. Integrated analyses characterize temporal regulatory dynamics and introduce a dynamic score to identify lineage-specific regulatory subnetworks, revealing hundreds of dynamic regulons and co-regulatory modules. We identify both known and novel candidate regulators that underlie neuronal differentiation and regional identity across the human brain and uncovered evolutionary divergence in neurogenic GRNs that distinguishes neurogenesis in humans from other species. Experimental characterization of the candidate neurogenic regulator ILF2 provides evidence for its role in neurogenesis. Furthermore, mapping disease-associated genes onto this resource reveals gene regulatory dynamics linked to 30 neurological disorders and traits, including autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, intellectual disability, and microcephaly. Our study provides a comprehensive cross-species and cross-regional atlas of neurogenic gene regulatory networks and their temporal dynamics. This resource facilitates the discovery of key regulators of early neuronal development, offers insights into the evolution of human brain regulatory programs, and enables the investigation of disease-associated regulatory mechanisms. The resource is freely accessible through an interactive online platform.

works.title: ROMET-RNA benchmarks and selects RNA 3D structures using multiple predictors and alignment strategies
works.abstract: Accurate prediction of RNA tertiary structure is essential for understanding RNA function, yet systematic, controlled benchmarking and integration of RNA three-dimensional structure prediction methods, particularly with respect to multiple sequence alignment strategies used by deep learning models, remain limited. Here, we present ROMET-RNA, an automated benchmarking framework and meta-selection toolkit that benchmarks eleven state-of-the-art RNA structure predictors within a standardized workflow and evaluates three complementary MSA pipelines, rMSA, RNAcmap3 MARS, and Infernal RNAcentral. Model selection is performed using a consensus scoring strategy combining TM-scoreRNA based structural similarity with the deep learning derived statistical potential lociPARSE. Benchmarking across four non-redundant test sets comprising 205 RNAs, including CASP15, RNA Puzzles, and recent PDB structures, demonstrates that ROMET-RNA consistently selects more accurate models than individual methods would on its own and we confirm that this is not an artefact of training-test overlap. Further analysis reveals that coevolutionary information substantially improves accuracy, that optimal MSA strategies are method specific, and that MSA depth exhibits a nonlinear relationship with performance. ROMET-RNA provides an open-source standardized framework that enhances RNA 3D structure model selection, supporting advances in RNA structural biology and genomics.

works.title: A new phased assembly of the Antarctic spiny plunderfish provides novel insights into the evolution of the notothenioid radiation
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Notothenioids are a well characterised species flock endemic to the Antarctic and an important model group for studying genome adaptation to extreme cold. A new reference assembly and clade-wide comparative genomic analysis allow for investigation of cryonotothenioid evolution and the appearance of novel functionalities linked to cold adaptation. RESULTS: A new phased assembly of a model notothenioid, Harpagifer antarcticus, demonstrated low levels of haplotypic variability across the genome. Nevertheless, numerous insertions from multiple LINE-L2 clades were found, suggesting ongoing transposition with potential contribution to speciation. Contrary to expectations the afgp locus was highly similar between haplotypes, except for large length allelic variants of afgp genes. Analysis suggests a model for the afgp locus expansion in H. antarcticus through segmental tandem duplications involving two pairs of afgp genes at time. Syntenic reconstruction of genomes from across the clade demonstrates conserved macrosyntenic relationships and group specific chromosomal fusions of notothenioids. Quantification of genome gain and transposition rates during cryonotothenioid diversification showed a first ancestral slow genome expansion concurrent with historic temperature drops. This was followed by lineage-specific massive peaks of genomic gain and transposition activity. Finally, we identified a set of genes that underwent ancestral diversifying selection and acquired novel conserved non-coding elements during the cryonotothenioid emergence. These were related to antioxidants and proteostasis, which may have facilitated the notothenioid Antarctic radiation. CONCLUSIONS: Diversifying selection and genomic gain linked to transposon activity are primary contributors to lineage-specific evolutionary dynamics through the clade which facilitated adaptation to life in the cold.

works.title: The contribution of short tandem repeats to splicing variation in the human prefrontal cortex
works.abstract: Abstract Background Splicing disruption has been implicated in a range of heritable phenotypes, including numerous psychiatric and neurological disorders. Recent studies have focused largely on single nucleotide polymorphisms or short indels. Despite growing evidence that genetic variation at short tandem repeats (STRs) influences splicing, large-scale studies of STR-mediated splicing in the brain have been limited by low sample sizes of available RNA-seq data or exclusion of certain classes of STRs. Results Here, we leverage deep RNA-seq and SNP array data from 336 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) samples collected by the Human Brain Collection Core. We identify 51,343 unique STRs for which copy number is significantly associated with one or multiple alternative splicing events of nearby genes (spliceSTRs). We prioritize and characterize candidate causal spliceSTRs using three orthogonal fine-mapping strategies, identifying 1,313 high-confidence fine-mapped spliceSTRs, and further find strong associations between copy number of certain repeat units and binding of specific RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). Co-localization analyses using summary statistics from genome-wide association studies for 6 brain-related disorders identified multiple signals that may be driven by fine-mapped spliceSTRs, including a previously identified ( GT ) n repeat that is a spliceSTR for PLEKHA1 associated with Alzheimer’s disease as well as a newly identified ( AGG ) n spliceSTR in SEPTIN3 co-localized with schizophrenia. Conclusions Our findings highlight the role of STRs in regulating alternative splicing in the human brain, suggesting a general relationship between STR polymorphism and RBP-mediated splicing events, and identify specific spliceSTRs detected by co-localization analysis as candidate causal variants for brain-related disorders.

works.title: Germline structural variation involving gynecologic and breast cancers reveals polygenic signatures of tumor mutational load
works.abstract: Germline structural variants (SVs), genomic variants involving larger segments of the human genome, are understudied in the context of cancer. The impact of germline variants on the regulation of specific genes is highly dependent on tissue and cellular context, necessitating focused, multi-omics studies by cancer tissue of origin. Here, we combine patient germline SV data with tumor multi-omics profiling across 2006 breast and gynecologic cancers, including breast, cervical, ovarian, uterine endometrial, and uterine carcinosarcoma tumors, to determine the extent to which germline SV patterns influence the tumor molecular landscape. Rare germline SV events predicted to disrupt specific cancer-relevant genes cumulatively affect approximately 29% of patients. We find thousands of genes exhibit significant associations between nearby germline SV breakpoints and altered tumor gene expression or DNA methylation. These associations are either specific to tumor type or shared across multiple tumor types and involve numerous cancer-relevant genes. We also identify widespread associations of germline SV patterns with tumor somatic mutational load, including copy number alteration and somatic structural variation, with similar patterns observed in additional cancer cohorts beyond gynecologic and breast cancers. Notably, we find a germline deletion SV spanning UGT2B17 (involving 36% of patients), is associated with reduced UGT2B17 expression and lower tumor mutational load. Germline SV-associated dysregulation in known cancer susceptibility genes or established cancer related genes considerably expands the spectrum of patients with evidence of a germline contribution to cancer development or progression. The patient’s genetic background may influence tumor characteristics, including somatic mutational load.

works.title: Non-invasive genomic sampling uncovers novel connectivities and origins of confiscated gorillas
works.abstract: Abstract Background Gorillas are a group of African great apes with two species and four subspecies that are currently critically endangered or endangered. Previous studies analyzing the genetics of wild gorillas from non-invasive samples such as faeces or hair have analysed short mitochondrial or nuclear markers, which may not reflect the wider nuclear genome. Recent technical advances in target capture hybridisation, enrich the endogenous DNA content of non-invasive samples, allowing contiguous genomic regions to be sequenced. Results Here, we generate georeferenced genetic dataset from faecal and hair samples of 280 wild gorillas, sampled from three of the four gorilla subspecies, across large parts of their present-day distributions. With this expanded representation of gorilla genetic diversity in the wild, we detect three population clusters in western lowland gorillas, with the Sangha River and its affluents acting as significant barriers to gene flow. We reconstruct patterns of past population connectivity between western lowland gorillas in the north-eastern distribution range and Cross River gorillas, which may have been facilitated by a migration corridor also used by the Central and Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee subspecies. Finally, we predict the geographic origins of wild-born gorillas, achieving a mean prediction error of 65 km, with a population-level resolution for mountain gorillas and some populations of western lowland gorillas. Conclusion Our work characterises fine-scale population structure in western lowland gorillas, which will be informative for future conservation strategies. This proof-of-concept in predicting geographic locations of wild gorillas, will be useful for future applications to geolocalise trafficked or rescued gorillas.

works.title: Genome-Wide DNA methylation profiling of tissue-plasma pairs identifies Novel cfDNA biomarkers for the diagnosis of gastric cancer
works.abstract: Screening for gastric cancer (GC) is critical for improving patient survival, yet current clinical methods suffer from invasiveness and limited sensitivity. The aim of this study is to develop a machine learning model for the non-invasive diagnosis of GC using the whole-genome methylation profile of circulating free DNA (cfDNA) in plasma. Plasma cfDNA from 61 patients with GC and 29 healthy controls. First, whole‑genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) was performed on 29 paired GC and adjacent normal tissues to identify differentially methylated regions (DMRs). These tissue DMRs were then mapped to plasma cfDNA methylation data, yielding 32 stable DMRs that changed consistently in both tissues and plasma. Using LASSO and Random Forest (RF) algorithms, eight core diagnostic markers were selected. Four machine learning algorithms (Support Vector Machine, RF, K-Nearest Neighbor, Naïve Bayes) were used to build diagnostic models. WGBS revealed global hypomethylation and CpG island hypermethylation in GC, consistent with plasma cfDNA methylation patterns. The RF model built on the eight cfDNA methylation markers (annotated to genes including ATP8A2) performed best, achieving AUC values of 0.978 and 0.938 in the training and independent test sets, respectively, with an accuracy of 88.46%, sensitivity of 94.44%, and specificity of 75.00%. After adjusting for age, the model achieved an AUC of 0.924 on the test set, still demonstrating high discriminatory performance. Functional analysis implicated these markers in pathways such as phagocytosis and axon guidance, and showed significant correlation with immune cell infiltration. Notably, these core DMRs are not covered by the probes on the methylation arrays (450K and EPIC v2), highlighting the advantage of WGBS for novel biomarker discovery. In conclusion, tissue-plasma concordance analysis identified a panel of plasma cfDNA methylation biomarkers with strong diagnostic potential. The resulting RF model provides a promising non-invasive strategy for GC screening.

works.title: Early NOTCH1 mutation is positively selected but epistatically suppresses evolution of later esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma drivers
works.abstract: Abstract Background Somatic mutations commonly accumulate in histologically normal tissues and contribute to cancer development. However, many mutations that are common in normal tissue are also found in cancers from the same organ, making their role in malignant progression unclear. To address this, we asked whether such mutations increase cell proliferation and survival to different degrees at different steps of esophageal tumor development, and whether they alter selection for other driver mutations. Methods We used a quantitative evolutionary framework to distinguish underlying mutation rate from selection across two steps of esophageal development: from organogenesis to clonal histologically normal esophageal epithelium, and from that tissue to esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma. Analyzing sequence data from 2171 samples, we estimated step-specific selection on recurrent somatic mutations, corresponding to increased cellular division and survival, and tested whether mutations in one gene earlier in the trajectory changed selection for mutations on another. We additionally examined somatic copy-number alterations and single-cell transcriptomic profiles to contextualize these evolutionary patterns within broader genomic and cellular changes during progression. Results NOTCH1 mutations were strongly selected during the clonal expansion of histologically normal esophageal epithelium, explaining their high prevalence in that tissue. However, for the first time, we show that there is little to no positive selection for NOTCH1, NOTCH2, and FAT1 mutations during progression from clonal histologically normal esophageal tissue to esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma in humans, leading to a conclusion that these alterations promote clonal expansion in normal tissue, but do not drive malignant progression from established normal clones. Moreover, we provide a somatic genetic basis for this step-specific effect: we demonstrate for the first time that mutations in NOTCH1 exhibit antagonistic epistasis with mutations of TP53 and RB1 , reducing selection for these key tumor suppressor alterations during tumor development. Consistent with this model, copy-number alterations associated with later ESCC progression were more strongly selected in TP53 -mutant samples, supporting the idea that TP53 disruption promotes a genomic context more permissive for malignant evolution. Conclusions Early somatic mutations can promote clonal expansion in normal tissue without promoting cancer, and in some cases may limit progression by reducing selection for later driver events. NOTCH1 and other genes can shape evolutionary trajectories in ways that ultimately constrain malignant progression. By separating mutation rate from selection, quantifying step-specific genetic interactions, and considering broader changes in genomic and cellular context, our study shows that the effects of recurrent mutations depend strongly on disease stage and mutational context—what promotes clonal expansion in normal tissue may later impede growth or survival in tumors. These insights underscore the need for precision strategies that account for the shifting fitness landscape across premalignant and malignant stages, informing early detection, prevention, and therapeutic prioritization.

works.title: Decoding coupled epigenetic-fragmentomic signals in circulating cell-free DNA for interpretable cancer diagnosis
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) whole-genome methylation sequencing enables simultaneous characterization of DNA methylation and fragmentomic features for cancer detection. However, it remains unclear whether methylation library preparation faithfully preserves fragmentomic signals, how methylation and fragmentation are biologically coupled, and how these two modalities can be systematically integrated. METHODS: We systematically evaluated the preservation of cfDNA fragmentomic features in whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) and enzymatic methyl sequencing (EM-seq) relative to conventional whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We next investigated the biological relationship between methylation and fragmentation and delineated methylation haplotype blocks (MHBs) directly from plasma cfDNA as biologically interpretable units for organizing multimodal cfDNA signals. Guided by these findings, we developed multimodal diagnostic models integrating complementary methylation and fragmentomic features. RESULTS: Canonical cfDNA fragmentomic patterns were partially preserved across methylation sequencing protocols, although the degree of preservation varied among individual features. DNA methylation levels were associated with characteristic fragment length and end-motif patterns. Plasma-derived MHBs exhibited tissue-associated regulatory features and distinct patterns of chromatin accessibility, repeat enrichment, and methylation heterogeneity, providing biologically interpretable units for integrated cfDNA analysis. Within these regions, methylation and fragmentomic signals exhibited coordinated yet complementary patterns. Leveraging this framework, we developed Fragmentomics And Methylation Ensemble (FAME), an interpretable multimodal model integrating MHB-centered methylation and fragmentomic features for cancer detection and tissue-of-origin prediction, and further extended it with complementary genome-wide methylation and fragmentomic features to generate a genome-wide-augmented FAME model (FAME-GW). Across cross-validation, independent validation, and comparisons with THEMIS (THorough Epigenetic Marker Integration Solution), SPOT-MAS (screening for the presence of tumor by methylation and size), and DELFI (DNA evaluation of fragments for early interception), FAME-based models achieved robust diagnostic performance, with FAME providing a compact and interpretable representation and FAME-GW delivering the strongest overall predictive performance. CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrates that cfDNA whole-genome methylation sequencing partially preserves informative fragmentomic signals and establishes plasma-derived MHBs as biologically interpretable units for organizing and integrating complementary methylation and fragmentomic information. This framework provides insight into the coupling of epigenetic and fragmentomic information and an effective strategy for interpretable cfDNA-based cancer diagnosis.

works.title: Accurate detection of sub-1% frequency somatic mutations by whole-genome sequencing
works.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
works.abstract: Continuous advances in read accuracy have positioned bulk whole-genome sequencing as a promising approach for somatic mutation discovery in research and clinical settings, but its utility for detecting low-frequency mutations in high-coverage data has not been thoroughly assessed. We utilized an experimental design featuring (1) primary human fibroblasts with naturally occurring mutations and expanded subclonal populations, (2) induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines corresponding to subclones, and (3) additional iPSC lines originating from other fibroblasts from the same donor, enabling comprehensive evaluation of mutation detection across analytical methods and sequencing depths. Mutations discovered in iPSC lines defined positive control mutations ranging from 0.1% to 25% variant allele fraction (VAF) and negative (i.e., absent) control mutations in fibroblasts. Using the negative controls, we determined PacBio and AVITI as the most accurate sequencing platforms in "easy" (i.e., reliably accessible by short reads) and "non-easy" genomic regions, respectively. AVITI was also the most accurate for indel sequencing. We benchmarked mutation detection in fibroblasts in "easy" regions using ∼1,360× Illumina short-read data for mutation discovery and combined ∼600× PacBio and AVITI data for confirmation. Our analyses demonstrated accurate and specific detection of point mutations below 1% VAF and non-homopolymer indels down to 1% VAF. Homopolymer indels could be reliably detected only at VAF >3%. Mutation detection was degraded in postmortem samples, for which we provide recommendations for additional filtering and data-quality assessment. Finally, we show that combining ∼200× coverage across tissues from a donor is a feasible strategy for detecting developmental mutations shared across tissues.
